descriptions.aions_core/AIONS_ULTIMATE_UNIFIED.py: This file assembles a complete artificial intelligence system from multiple specialized components into one unified command center. It loads memory storage (CBMS with Korean compression keys), a symbolic addressing system (Hangul codes), tournament scoring (CRLA), stored facts, a conversation enhancer, a math solver, and other tools, then answers user questions by routing them through this pipeline: first trying math if it looks mathematical, then checking stored facts, then querying the main knowledge base with Korean pattern matching and conversation refinement, and finally giving a soft refusal if nothing matches. The system tracks statistics including total queries, success rate, average latency, and compression ratios, saving them to disk. It accepts queries as text strings and returns structured responses with confidence scores, which sources were consulted, and how fast they came back. It talks to memory files, chunks stored as JSON, facts databases, and speaks with the language enhancement layers to make answers more natural. Someone would ask about this when building a conversational AI or when they need one system that coordinates between knowledge base searches, symbolic addressing, and natural language generation.
This file runs a production-ready system that compresses Polish and technical words into syllable patterns for faster neural processing. It loads a special version of the Phi-3 language model that has been tuned to recognize Korean linguistic patterns, then takes text input and breaks it into syllables that have meaning, assigns each a color code and semantic label, and processes them through the neural network to produce an understanding of what the text means with an efficiency score. The core pieces are: a dictionary of known syllable patterns and their meanings, a function that splits words into these patterns by checking the longest matches first, a function that maps each syllable to a data block with Korean mapping, and a final response generator that combines all the semantic pieces. Input is Polish or English text phrases; output is a JSON file containing the original text, syllable breakdown, compression ratios, semantic meanings, and overall system efficiency percentages. It talks to PyTorch for neural operations, reads safetensors model weights from disk, and writes the final production results to a JSON output file. Someone working with this would use it to speed up language processing for a language model by compressing complex words into their semantic building blocks.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_core.py: This file contains a reasoning engine that mimics how humans think through problems by breaking them down and following logical chains. It starts with understanding what the question is asking, creates a plan with smaller goals, executes each step while collecting evidence, reflects on how well the reasoning worked, and learns from the process. The main pieces are Thought nodes representing individual reasoning steps, Goals representing what needs to be accomplished, and WorkingMemory holding the current thinking context. The engine uses connection to an existing knowledge base (CBMS) to find relevant information, applies different reasoning strategies like deductive, inductive, and analogical thinking, and tracks confidence in its conclusions. Questions come in as text, and the output is a detailed response with the chain of reasoning shown, along with a confidence score and meta-analysis of the reasoning quality.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_evolution.py: This file manages automatic self-improvement for an artificial intelligence system by tracking what it does well and what it struggles with, then proposing and testing changes to make it better. It keeps a history of performance on eight different skills—like how fast it responds, how accurate its confidence predictions are, and how well it learns from examples—and when performance drops, it suggests improvement strategies such as doing deeper reasoning, trying new ideas, or consolidating what it already knows. The main pieces are: data structures for storing performance measurements over time, a list of predefined improvement strategies with success rates, functions to analyze performance from interaction data, functions to select which strategies to apply based on weaknesses, and a history log of all evolution attempts. Input is feedback about how well the system performed on tasks; output is improvement plans, updated metrics, strategy success rates, and a readiness assessment (Initial/Developing/Competent/Advanced/Expert). It interacts with AGI core and learning modules to apply changes, reads and writes configuration files in JSON format, and keeps all state in memory with the ability to save it. Users would think of this as the part of the system that makes the AI get smarter by learning from its mistakes.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_existing_models.py: This file acts as a hub that discovers and manages language models already installed on the computer—specifically Mistral-7B, Phi-3 (modified for Korean), and Bielik. It loads each model only when needed, using either llama.cpp for compressed formats or the transformers library for PyTorch models, keeping only one model in memory at a time to save RAM. The file includes Korean syllable compression that reduces text size using patterns, and chunk loading from CBMS (code book memory system) JSON and binary files. When you ask it a question, it picks the best model based on what you're asking about, retrieves relevant chunks from memory, and generates an answer. An ensemble version runs multiple models and picks the best response. The system tracks how fast each query runs and what chunks were used.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_learning.py: This system teaches itself by studying past conversations and improving what it knows. It works like a student reviewing notes after class — when an interaction ends, it examines the question, the answer, and feedback to extract useful patterns and spot gaps in knowledge. The main pieces track learned patterns (the rules it discovers work well), concept relationships (how ideas connect to each other), and interactions (every Q&A it processes). Information flows in as conversations happen, and the system stores what it learns in an SQLite database with separate files for knowledge chunks. It also talks to the core memory system and to Korean compression tools that help it organize information efficiently. The system can consolidate overlapping knowledge, suggest follow-up questions to fill gaps, and generate insights about what works best.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_neural_backprop.py: This file implements a neural network system that can learn from feedback by tracking how errors flow backward through its layers, allowing it to adjust its thinking process. It combines several neural building blocks: an embedder that converts text chunks into learnable vectors, a multi-hop reasoning graph that combines knowledge to answer questions with attention to which knowledge matters most, and differentiable memory that can read and write using soft addressing so gradients can flow through everything. The main components are embedding layers for tokenizing and positioning, transformer encoders for processing, a multi-step reasoning network with gated recurrent units, memory read/write controllers with attention mechanisms, and loss functions for confidence, knowledge consistency, and continuous improvement. Input is a query string and knowledge chunks as dictionaries; output is a response embedding, confidence score, and the reasoning path it took. The system runs on GPU if available (CUDA), saves checkpoints to disk, and analyzes gradient flow to detect learning problems like vanishing or exploding gradients. Someone using this would see it as the trainable thinking engine that improves by comparing its outputs against ground truth feedback.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_soft_retrieval.py: This file implements differentiable retrieval with gradient flow—a machine learning technique where the system can learn and improve how it finds relevant information. The retriever uses a two-stage process: first it filters candidate chunks using BM25 (a fast text-matching algorithm), then it scores them with learnable embeddings that can be tuned through backpropagation. The main components are the BM25 filter for initial candidate selection, a ChunkEmbedder that turns text into numerical vectors using transformer neural networks, and a SoftRetriever that computes soft attention weights over candidates and mixes them into a final context representation. The code also includes a CitationCoverageLoss that penalizes responses that don't cite the source documents, encouraging proper attribution. Input consists of document chunks and a query string; output includes attention weights showing which chunks were most relevant, the candidate embeddings, and optionally gradient flow diagnostics. The retriever talks to PyTorch for neural computation and validates that gradients can flow backward through the entire retrieval pipeline for end-to-end training.
descriptions.aions_core/agi_unified.py: This file brings together all the thinking, learning, and evolution components into one complete system, routing queries to the right processor depending on the mode selected. It can use pure symbolic reasoning (logical steps), pure neural processing (machine learning), or both together for a hybrid approach. The main components are the reasoning core (logical thinking), learning pipeline (gets smarter from interactions), evolution system (improves strategies), neural backprop system (if available), and CBMS memory storage. Queries come in through the main process method, and the system decides which components to use based on the mode and what is available. It tracks how confident each approach is, runs learning and evolution in background threads, saves state to disk, and reports its health status showing which components are working.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_agent_layer.py: This file provides a safe execution layer where an AI agent can run tool-based tasks without directly touching the computer's core systems. It defines a whitelist of specific tools (reading files, writing files, listing directories, web searching, Python evaluation, memory queries) each with a risk rating (safe, low, medium, high, critical) and execution limits. When a task is requested, this layer plans what steps are needed, checks that each tool is whitelisted and hasn't exceeded its per-session quota, asks for human confirmation if the step is risky, then executes it, logs what happened to an audit file, and stops immediately if something fails. Input is a task goal and optional context parameters; output is a structured result showing which steps succeeded or failed, how long each took, and a complete audit trail. This talks to AIONS memory (for knowledge queries), a hybrid retrieval system (for context), and saves knowledge to JSON files in the data directory. Someone would use this when they want an AI agent that can carry out multi-step instructions safely without accidentally deleting files or making uncontrolled network calls.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_crla_reformed.py: This file combines cleaned seed data from reformed CBMS with a tournament system (CRLA) for picking the best answer. When you ask a question, it first tries to answer directly from stored facts. If there's no direct answer and the memory system retrieves too many chunks (panic threshold), it generates multiple candidate answers, scores each one using a metric formula, runs them through a tournament, and picks the winner. The winning answer gets saved as a derivation with timestamp and trace showing which candidates were considered. High-confidence direct answers are saved as facts. The system detects when it's overwhelmed with too much information (panic) and switches strategies. The file imports existing modules for memory, CBMS integration, and CRLA scoring, testing the complete workflow.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_hybrid_retrieval.py: A search system that combines three different ways of finding information—keyword matching using BM25 scoring, vector similarity search, and intelligent reranking with machine learning models—to give better search results than any single method alone. It loads knowledge from an existing AIONS system and other sources, processes search queries by running them through all three methods, then merges and ranks the results to show the most relevant information first. The system tracks statistics on how often each search method is used and how fast searches happen. It takes search queries as input and returns ranked lists of relevant documents with scores and metadata about which method found each result. It integrates with the original AIONS knowledge base, vector search databases, and optionally uses cross-encoder models to rerank results for better quality.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_monitoring_dashboard.py: This file is a production-ready monitoring system that watches over an AIONS installation and makes sure everything works. It runs a comprehensive test suite across core, vector search, and hybrid retrieval components, checking that each one responds correctly. The monitoring system tracks how fast queries run, measures success rates, and logs errors. A health check verifies each component is operational. Performance benchmarking runs queries repeatedly and calculates percentiles (95th, 99th) to understand response time distribution. All test results, performance metrics, and error logs get saved to files with timestamps. The system generates a human-readable report showing which components are working, what tests passed or failed, and how the system is performing overall, outputting everything as JSON and text summaries.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_reactor.py: This file implements a complete orchestration engine that executes learning goals, creates and manages micro-skills as JSON-based packages, and evaluates performance throughout the process. The main pieces are the AdvancedSkillForge class which loads, creates, and tracks skills from disk; the FinalReactorCRLA class which orchestrates multi-round learning with real-time evaluation; and various task execution methods that handle research, simulation, and distillation work. The system reads goal definitions from YAML files containing task lists and deliverables, loads or creates skill JSON files from a skills directory, and integrates a memory graph engine for concept expansion and CBMS retrieval system for knowledge lookup. It outputs comprehensive results as JSON including skill creation records, performance metrics, and evaluation reports saved to disk. The reactor talks to a memory graph system, CBMS knowledge storage, an evaluator engine for quality scoring, and saves skills registry and performance data to the file system. Users would search for this when looking to build a complete learning pipeline that trains systems to accomplish complex multi-step goals while automatically creating reusable knowledge blocks.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_reformed_integration.py: A question-answering system that loads factual information from organized seed data files covering topics like capitals, math, science, programming, and history, and combines it with a memory management system to answer user questions. It implements a step-by-step process: first checking for direct matches in seed data, then looking up more complex knowledge, and finally falling back to a memory system for unknown topics. The system handles aliases by replacing one word with another, applies patches for known incorrect answers, and supports Polish language queries. Input is a user question, output is a structured response with the answer, confidence score, and the source layer where the answer came from. It integrates with seed data files organized by topic and a memory system for handling questions the basic data doesn't cover.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_smart_guardrail.py: This file prevents the AI system from making up answers by checking whether a user's question has supporting information in the knowledge base. It loads two sources of truth: a legacy indexed database and a new facts database stored as JSON lines, then scores how well the question matches what it knows, returning either evidence from the knowledge base or a refusal message when information is missing. The main components include a tokenizer that breaks text into searchable words, a document loader that merges both knowledge sources into memory with index structures mapping each token to relevant documents, and a retrieval function that finds matching documents by counting how many query words appear in each stored document. Data flows in as natural language questions and flows out as either approved answers with source references or explicit refusals, and the system talks to both a binary posting index file (kr_postings.bin) and a line-delimited facts file (facts.jsonl). Someone searching for information about hallucination prevention, fact-checking systems, or grounding AI responses in real data would find this file relevant.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_style_parameters.py: This file implements a response styling system that adjusts how text sounds and reads without changing what it says—making responses sound professional or casual, brief or detailed, confident or uncertain. The main components are the StyleParameters dataclass that holds five numeric values controlling tone (formality, brevity, technicality, friendliness, confidence), the StyleProfile enum defining preset combinations, and the StyleController class that applies style transformations to text through regex-based word replacement and sentence manipulation. The system accepts plain text input and user-specified style preferences, then outputs modified text with the same factual content but different tone, along with metadata about which style was applied. It reads from and modifies text strings in memory without persistent storage. The file optionally integrates with a natural language wrapper module but works standalone. Users would look here when they need to adjust the personality or formality level of AI responses for different audiences or contexts.
descriptions.aions_core/aions_vector_enhancement.py: This file adds semantic search using LanceDB, a vector database that finds information by meaning rather than exact words. It connects to an existing LanceDB instance used by Kiro (another system in the environment), specifically looking for a table containing knowledge documents. When you search, it scans the database and returns relevant results with similarity scores. The file discovers what tables exist and connects to the main knowledge table. It provides statistics about the database like how many rows are stored. Without the embedding model loaded separately, it does basic limit-scanned retrieval instead of true semantic search, so full text-to-vector search requires additional setup. The connection shows table names and row counts proving it's communicating with the vector database.
descriptions.aions_core/api.py: This file starts a web server that listens for incoming questions and routes them to the unified AIONS core system for processing. It uses FastAPI to create HTTP endpoints and forces all transformer libraries to work offline from cached models to avoid network issues. The main pieces are: startup code that initializes the AIONS v2 system with all Phase 4 components enabled (vector search, hybrid logic, agent system, styling, monitoring), a health check that runs on startup to verify everything loads correctly, and three HTTP endpoints—one to answer queries, one to check status, and one to report root health. Input comes as JSON with a query string field; output is a JSON response from the processing system, or an error message if something fails. It imports the unified_core module from the local directory and also tries to handle import errors by appending to sys.path, talks to all AIONS subsystems through the aions object, and returns HTTP status codes (503 for not ready, 500 for runtime error, 200 for success). A developer would use this as the entry point to talk to the AIONS system from external clients over HTTP.
descriptions.aions_core/cbms_curve_machine.py: This file breaks down complex AI operations into small, reusable pieces called kernels, each performing one specific task like searching, compressing, scoring, or embedding. It maintains a registry of these atomic operations and creates execution graphs that show which kernels must run in sequence to solve a problem, and it includes real model weights and paths on disk. The main pieces include kernel definitions (each describing what it does and what inputs and outputs it needs), a weights manifest tracking where actual neural network model files live and how big they are, and graph builders that compose kernels into complete pipelines for retrieval, reasoning, and even training with backpropagation. Configuration data describes 10+ kernels and 6 weight files flow in from registry initialization, while kernel definitions and execution graphs flow out to JSON files in a local directory structure, and the system references weights stored on the E: drive including Phi-3 models, Mistral, and Korean-modified language models. Anyone looking for how to modularize large systems, describe computation as composable operations, or understand model inference orchestration would search for this.
descriptions.aions_core/cbms_memory.py: This implements a memory system for AI agents based on chunking and concept mapping—treating knowledge like a collection of encyclopedia entries that can be stored, retrieved, and connected. The CBMSMemory class maintains a directory of JSON chunks representing facts or concepts, indexes them by concept names, and provides Korean-style syllable-based key indexing for fast lookups when enabled. When asked a question, the system extracts relevant concepts, retrieves matching chunks using Korean keys or concept mapping, optionally applies critical term boosting for important identifiers, and synthesizes an answer by combining the found knowledge. Input includes user queries and metadata like concept tags; output is a synthesized answer with references to the chunks that were used plus timing information. The system persists everything to disk in a chunks directory and writes a thinking log recording each retrieval session with reasoning steps. It talks to optional modules like the codebook engine for Esperanto/CBMS symbolic indexing and hangul addressing for multilingual support.
descriptions.aions_core/claude_aions_bridge.py: This file connects the AIONS knowledge retrieval system with Claude's language model to provide fast, accurate answers. It takes user questions and tries to find matching information from a vector database first (the CBMS system), and if that fails, falls back to the language model for help. The main job is measuring how well the hybrid approach works by tracking response time, what information chunks were used, and overall performance quality. It receives a query string as input and returns a response dictionary containing the answer text, the source that provided it, how long it took in milliseconds, how many reference pieces were used, and whether performance was excellent or good. The code imports and calls the smart_cbms_response function to do the actual retrieval work. Someone searching for how Claude integrates with the AIONS system, or looking for where hybrid retrieval responses come from, would find this file.
descriptions.aions_core/evaluator_engine.py: This file grades how well the system performed on a complete run of tasks, calculating scores across multiple dimensions and writing results to a scoreboard. It evaluates each task looking at response time, whether information came directly from stored knowledge, quality of the answer, how many concepts were used, and how much the answer was enhanced beyond basic retrieval. The scoreboard CSV captures timestamp, goal identifier, round number, latency, direct retrieval rate, quality score, concepts used, skills created, and overall performance grade. The evaluator calculates an overall score from zero to one hundred using weighted formulas that emphasize different aspects, assigns letter grades from F (poor) to A+ (excellent), and generates readable performance reports for human review.
descriptions.aions_core/ingest_cbms_data.py: A data loading tool that reads JSON files from a specific folder and uploads them into a vector database (LanceDB) so they can be searched by similarity matching. It processes chunks of text one at a time in batches of 100, converts each text into a numerical representation using a machine learning model, and stores these embeddings in the database alongside the original text and file paths. The tool tracks progress with a progress bar and measures how fast the loading is happening. Input is JSON files containing text content, output is vectors stored in LanceDB with associated metadata. It communicates with the sentence-transformers library to generate embeddings and writes the results into a vector table.
descriptions.aions_core/memory_graph_engine.py: This file creates a map of how different ideas relate to each other to make searching faster and smarter. Think of it like a spider web where each concept is a point and the threads show which ideas connect. The main pieces load or build a graph from a JSON file, find related concepts by walking those connections, expand a question to include related topics, and assign importance scores to different concepts. It takes in search queries and outputs both expanded searches and tags for categorizing knowledge. The system reads and writes a graph file in JSON format, and it can integrate with the main memory system to improve how it retrieves stored information. When someone searches for a topic, this engine automatically thinks of related topics they might have also meant, making results more complete.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_direct_server.py: This is a web server that listens for questions and answers them using a compressed memory system. It combines several parts: math solving for arithmetic, pattern matching for common greetings, a memory retrieval system for knowledge-based questions, and a fallback to the internet for topics it does not know. The server accepts chat messages as JSON over HTTP, processes them through multiple routes (math first, then conversational shortcuts, then deep searching), and returns answers as formatted text. It talks to the memory system, a facts database, several optional enhancement modules for making responses more natural, and optionally fetches information from the web. The server tracks performance, quality assurance results, and consciousness patterns if those features are enabled. It runs constantly, waiting for requests on port 9000.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_doctor.py: This tool reads the chunk storage directory and reports on consistency problems—like files with corrupted JSON, missing fields, empty content, or broken references—similar to how a disk checker reports file system integrity issues. It performs read-only diagnostics: scanning all chunks, verifying they have required fields, checking for dangling references to non-existent chunks, detecting orphaned chunks nobody references, analyzing access counts to see if the system is actually using stored knowledge, and flagging schema drift where chunks have unexpected extra fields. Input is a directory path containing chunk JSON files; output is a list of findings organized by severity (critical, warning, info) with examples of each problem found. The tool produces JSON for programmatic use or human-readable text output, and can exit with an error code if critical issues are found. It only reads—never writes, deletes, or modifies anything—making it safe to run anytime, and serves as an early warning system to catch memory corruption before it affects retrieval.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_memory.py: An artificial intelligence memory system that chunks up and organizes knowledge into small pieces so an AI can recall relevant information quickly when answering questions. It saves knowledge chunks to disk with unique IDs, builds indexes using Korean-style syllable matching and optional symbolic codes for faster lookups, and has safeguards to prevent saving garbage or repetitive responses that aren't real knowledge. The system tracks what knowledge exists, generates thinking traces showing how it retrieved and synthesized information, and allows learning new things through a decision gate that rejects noise and echo. Input is knowledge to learn and questions to answer, output is retrieved information and synthesized responses. It stores chunks as JSON files and maintains a manifest of all knowledge with timestamps and access counts.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_outline.py: This file implements a progressive disclosure system for retrieving information from the CBMS (Code Book Memory System) storage. The mechanism splits knowledge retrieval into two phases to save context space: first, a lightweight skeleton of available chunks (summaries without full content), and second, full detailed content for only the selected chunks. The skeleton includes identifiers, concepts, character counts, access statistics, and summary lines, while actively tracking whether chunks are stored (active tier) or archived (parked tier). The system accepts search queries, concept filters, and budget constraints in characters to trim results by relevance score, and uses tokenization to skip common words in matching. The tool reads from disk directories containing JSON chunk files, calculates incoming reference degrees to weight important chunks, and returns results formatted as JSON or human-readable tables. Callers can request outline summaries for planning or drill deep into specific chunks for full content, making it possible to fit thousands of chunks' metadata into a small context window.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_purgatory.py: This file implements a three-stage lifecycle system for new knowledge chunks in the memory system—they start in purgatory (quarantine), get evaluated based on actual usage patterns, then either get promoted to active storage or parked in quarantine based on a scoring system. The core concept is that value is proven by whether someone actually reads the full chunk (a drill), not just whether it appears in search results. The main pieces are the Config class holding decision thresholds, a ledger registry tracking each chunk's history (admission date, drill count, session dates), utility functions for safe file movement and status judgment, and CLI commands for admitting chunks, recording usage, reviewing status, and executing promotion decisions. The system reads chunk JSON files from three directories (purgatory, active chunks, quarantine) and a ledger file tracking metadata, then moves files between directories and updates the ledger based on judgment verdicts. All file operations use safe atomic writes and never delete files—failed chunks are renamed to quarantine, never erased. This tool talks to the file system, the chunk storage directories, and the ledger tracking file. Users search for this when they need to ensure knowledge quality by preventing low-value telemetry and system output from cluttering the main memory store.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_symbolic_index.py: A lookup table that converts written text into symbolic codes so questions can be matched against stored knowledge using those codes instead of raw words. It builds itself by reading all stored knowledge chunks, converting each one's text into Esperanto (an international language), then encoding that into CBMS codes (compact symbolic representations). When you search, the tool converts your question to the same Esperanto-based codes, then looks up which knowledge chunks use those same codes, ranking them by how many codes matched. Input is knowledge chunks and a search query, output is ranked chunks sorted by match strength. It uses an Esperanto bridge library to handle language conversion and a codebook engine to manage the symbolic encoding system.
descriptions.aions_core/server/cbms_unified_server.py: This HTTP server on port 9000 answers questions using the CBMS knowledge system, optionally pulls in information from the internet when its knowledge runs low, and supports conversational features. It implements a chat endpoint that takes user messages, checks whether they might be math problems, tries pattern matching for common conversational topics, then uses CBMS retrieval and optional web search to compose answers. The main components are a CBMS memory loader (reading chunks and facts), a facts database handler, a Web RAG module that fetches live internet information when confidence drops, and a conversational knowledge base with pre-written patterns for greetings and capabilities. User messages enter via HTTP POST and responses exit as JSON with the answer text and optional source citations, the system reads CBMS memory files, accesses a network crawler when needed, and calls the math solver and conversation enhancer on a best-effort basis. A developer setting up a knowledge-based chatbot or needing to combine static knowledge with live web answers would look here.
descriptions.aions_core/server/codebook_engine.py: This file is a simple bidirectional translator between ordinary English-like text and a compact system of symbolic codes, using phrase matching rather than complex linguistics. It loads a codebook dictionary where each symbol (like 'K001') maps to multiple phrases and codes, then when encoding, it greedily marks the longest matching phrases in text as used (preventing double-counting) and outputs the list of symbols; when decoding, it takes symbols and outputs the text phrases they represent, joined together. Input is either text to encode or a list of codes to decode; output is the opposite form. It manages a two-way lookup table to avoid redundant scanning. This talks only to a JSON codebook file loaded at startup and uses no external services. Someone would ask for this when they need to compress conversations, questions, or knowledge into a code sequence that can be transmitted quickly or stored compactly, then expand it back when needed.
This module makes AI responses sound more natural and human-like instead of robotic or repetitive. It detects what type of question was asked (greeting, emotional, philosophical, creative, technical), and adjusts the response style to match. The main pieces include templates for different response types, emotional context detection, a system to track the conversation history, and synonym replacement to avoid sounding repetitive. The system takes in a basic response and a question, then outputs a warmer, more personalized version that includes appropriate emoticons, natural sentence starters, and context references. It remembers what was discussed before and can reference it later. It also profiles individual users and adapts tone based on their preferences, ranging from formal to casual.
descriptions.aions_core/server/conversation_memory.py: This file records and recalls conversations to give context for future responses and automatically summarize long discussions. It saves every exchange (question and answer) into date-stamped log files, extracts key topics and names mentioned, and periodically rolls up old summaries into consolidated records. Data flows in as user text and system responses, gets stored in JSON line files organized by session, and gets searched when generating context for new questions. It also detects when users introduce themselves and stores that as a user profile chunk. The system talks to the main memory system to create knowledge chunks from summaries, builds a searchable index of concepts, and rolls up batches of summaries when they reach a certain size. The system helps avoid repeating information and makes conversations feel continuous.
descriptions.aions_core/server/crla_core.py: This file implements a multi-candidate ranking system that generates multiple query-answering strategies, scores each one on six quality dimensions, and runs a tournament to select the best answer. The main pieces are the Candidate dataclass describing a query-answering approach with parameters, the CandidateResult dataclass holding six factor scores (facts coverage, determinism, latency, policy adherence, trace compactness, answer hygiene), and functions that simulate each candidate, calculate individual factor scores, run a bracket-tournament to pick a winner, and assemble final results. The system takes a query string and optional random seed, generates eight candidates with varying parameters, runs each through a CBMS memory engine measuring latency, scores on weighted factors, picks the best via tournament, and returns the winner's answer along with a ranked scoreboard of all candidates. It reads from a CBMS memory system (which provides chunk references and thinking traces), and outputs a JSON result dictionary with the final answer, all scores, and ranking data. Users would search for this when looking to run multiple approaches to a problem in parallel and pick the highest-quality result.
descriptions.aions_core/server/esperanto_bridge.py: This file provides a lightweight, deterministic way to normalize text by converting Polish and English phrases into Esperanto, creating a neutral, standardized representation for symbolic processing. It handles two directions: normalizing mixed-case text with irregular spacing into lowercase and consistent form, then mapping common Polish words and CBMS domain terms (like 'pamięć' → 'memoro' and 'turniej' → 'turniro') using a small hardcoded dictionary, and it provides a backward conversion that renders Esperanto back into Polish for display. The data flow takes in unstructured user text and outputs regularized Esperanto strings suitable for indexing and retrieval, while talking to no external systems—it's self-contained and designed to be safe without heavy dependencies. Someone building a multilingual knowledge system or needing a language-agnostic encoding scheme would find this useful.
descriptions.aions_core/server/facts_loader.py: This file checks how many known facts in storage are relevant to a given query by looking up key phrases in an index. It loads a facts index mapping key phrases to fact identifiers, then when given a query, builds the search keys from that query, looks up which facts match those keys, and counts unique facts found. The coverage method returns how many stored facts touched by the query keys, while coverage_hashed version only counts facts matched by hashed keys. The data structure is a simple JSON index file mapping key strings to lists of fact identifiers, allowing quick lookup to see whether the system has relevant stored knowledge for a question.
descriptions.aions_core/server/generator_cbms.py: This file builds structured answers by combining knowledge base chunks with question context. When someone asks a question, it retrieves relevant text passages from a chunked knowledge management system (CBMS), then formats them into a readable response that includes key points, conversation history, and performance metrics from a ranking system called CRLA. The main function takes a query and several optional inputs like retrieved chunk identifiers, conversation history, and ranking results, then outputs a formatted text string with numbered key points, optional context snippets, performance statistics, and source attribution. It talks to the CBMS system to fetch actual chunk content by identifier, and pulls scoring data from a CRLA ranking system. Someone would ask about this when they need to take search results and turn them into a polished answer with proper citations.
descriptions.aions_core/server/hangul_addressing.py: This file converts data into Korean Hangul characters for use as compact identifiers or addressing codes. It takes any text input, creates a SHA1 hash of it, and translates that hash into a sequence of Hangul syllables as a way to represent the data. The process involves converting each hexadecimal digit from the hash into a Korean character by calculating an offset from the base Hangul syllable. The main function accepts text and a length parameter, returning a string of Korean characters that uniquely represents the input. It uses only Python's built-in hashlib and character encoding, requiring no external dependencies. Someone would use this when they need a human-readable but compact way to reference data or create short codes for items in a system that supports Korean text.
descriptions.aions_core/server/korean_keys.py: This file creates searchable matching keys from text by extracting syllable-like patterns inspired by Korean writing conventions. When given a text input, it extracts all word tokens (alphanumeric sequences), then generates two types of key patterns: three-character substrings from the tokens themselves, and three-character groups extracted from SHA1 hashes of the tokens. Each key is prefixed with 'g:' for grammar-based keys or 'h:' for hash-based keys to distinguish the source. The function returns a set of all these keys for rapid matching against query keys. It talks to hashlib for cryptographic hashing and uses regex for token extraction. Someone would ask about this when they need fast approximate matching between search queries and text, or when building a search index that doesn't require exact keyword matching.
descriptions.aions_core/server/math_solver.py: This file recognizes when a user is asking a math question and attempts to solve it using heuristics that detect common problem patterns (like work-rate calculations, percentage changes, inventory tracking, and simple arithmetic). It first checks whether a question looks mathematical by finding digits and math-related keywords in multiple languages including Polish, English, and Esperanto, then runs the query through a series of specialized solvers, each handling a specific problem type—for instance, one solves 'Janet makes X eggs per day, eats Y, bakes Z, sells remainder at P dollars each' and another handles 'A percent increase of B'. The main pieces include a detector function, number extractors for both integers and floating point, and 20+ specialized solver functions that parse context, identify quantities and operations, and compute results. Text questions flow in, detection returns a boolean and either an integer answer or None, and the system reads keywords and patterns directly from the question string—it doesn't talk to external services, just applies pure logic. Anyone building a math word problem solver or studying how to extract meaning from language would look here.
descriptions.aions_core/server/pocket_qc.py: This provides lightweight quality checks on text and API results without heavy processing—a gatekeeper that marks outputs as pass, fail, or retry before they're stored as knowledge. For plain text, it checks for injection attacks like script tags and SQL keywords, and counts how many CBMS symbolic codes the text contains; if there are no attacks and some codes are present, the text passes. For structured results from AI comparison chains, it examines scores and determinism metrics; the result passes if it has acceptable scores, good determinism, isn't refused, and contains CBMS codes. Input is either raw text or a dictionary with winner scores and metadata; output is a verdict (pass/fail/retry) with details about what was checked. All verdicts get appended to a JSONL log file for tracking quality over time. The checks rely on optional CBMS symbolic encoding which may not always be available, but the system degrades gracefully—if the codebook isn't present, results still get verdicts based on other criteria.
descriptions.aions_core/server/refgraph.py: This file builds and maintains a flexible web of connections that tracks how different pieces of knowledge reference each other across the system. Instead of requiring exact matches for references (which breaks when files move or get renamed), it uses multiple fallback strategies that gradually lower their confidence levels: exact ID matches score highest at 1.0, manifest entries score 0.95, parked chunks score 0.80, normalized matches score 0.75, file path matches score 0.70, concept matches score 0.60, and token-based semantic overlap scores 0.30-0.55, with unresolved references kept as hints at 0.00. The system takes a directory path to chunks (individual knowledge units), an optional quarantine folder for archived pieces, a knowledge manifest file listing known IDs, and a project root directory for file indexing. It outputs statistics about how resolved the graph is, which chunks are at risk of depending on archived material, what other chunks reference a given ID, and more. It can be used from the command line with various flags like --stats, --who-refs, --resolve, --unresolved, or --build-index to generate detailed reports. The code has no external dependencies beyond Python's standard library and works with JSON files stored in folders. Someone wanting to verify that all their knowledge pieces are properly connected, find broken or weak links in the knowledge base, or check which documents depend on a specific piece of information would search for this file.
descriptions.aions_core/server/stylist.py: This file cleans up the formatting and whitespace in text answers without changing the actual facts or content. It normalizes spaces and newlines, fixes capitalization if needed, ensures bracketed source citations are on separate paragraphs, and then verifies that nothing important was lost by checking that all numbers, bracketed blocks, and structured elements are still present in the same quantities. The main pieces are: a whitespace normalization function that collapses multiple spaces and lines but preserves line breaks and structure, safety pattern checking that collects all numbers and bracketed sections before and after styling to compare them, and a main style_pass function that runs the cleanup and reports whether changes were made or if something went wrong. Input is a string answer that might have messy spacing or inconsistent formatting; output is the cleaned text plus a boolean saying if changes were applied plus a message code explaining success or failure. It uses regular expressions to find and verify patterns, doesn't call external systems, and is designed to be lightweight. Someone would use this when they have a wordy response that needs to look professional but the actual information must stay exactly correct.
descriptions.aions_core/server/ts_symbols.py: This file reads source code files in multiple programming languages, extracts all the function and class definitions and their relationships, and packages them as knowledge chunks ready to store in a searchable memory system. It uses tree-sitter, a parser that builds an abstract syntax tree from code, to walk through the code structure, identify named definitions and their line numbers, collect what other code each one calls or imports, and compute a hash of each body so you can tell later if something changed without re-parsing everything. The main pieces are: a Symbol class storing metadata about each code element with its name path, kind (function/class/method/etc), line range, signature, docstring, and soft references to other code; a SymbolIndex class that loads a file, parses it, and builds a queryable dictionary of symbols; and scanning functions that process entire directories. Input is a source file path in any supported language (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, C++, etc); output is an outline showing all symbols in the file with their kind and line numbers, or full chunk candidates that include docstrings and body code formatted for storage. It talks to tree-sitter-language-pack to parse code, reads source files from disk, and outputs JSON files with chunk candidates. Someone would use this to convert their codebase into a searchable knowledge base where the system can look up what any function does.
descriptions.aions_core/server/web_rag_cbms.py: A web-scraping integration that fetches current facts from the internet when the AI system doesn't have an answer stored locally, then injects those facts into memory as temporary knowledge chunks. It searches Wikipedia, Stack Overflow, GitHub, and documentation sites for information related to the user's question, extracts relevant sentences, scores them by how well they match the query, and converts them to memory chunks with source citations. The system is respectful to websites by pausing between requests and only trusts certain safe domains. Input is a user query that triggered a 'don't know' response, output is temporary memory chunks with citations to source URLs and relevance scores. It communicates with websites over HTTPS, parses HTML to extract clean text, and registers facts as temporary chunks in the memory system.
descriptions.aions_core/smart_cbms.py: This file speeds up question answering by trying to find the answer instantly in a cached knowledge system first, and only asking a larger language model if the cache doesn't have enough information. It measures how fast each stage takes, composes a very short prompt if it must call the language model, and combines the instant answer with the model's response into a final answer. The main pieces are: a CBMS memory object that instantly thinks through a question and returns matching knowledge chunks, logic to decide whether the cached answer is good enough or whether Bielik (a local language model) needs to be called, code that measures response time at each stage, a request formatter that sends only keywords to Bielik to keep the prompt tiny, and error handling if Bielik times out or is unavailable. Input is a natural language question; output is a string answer with timing information and a source attribution saying whether it came from CBMS cache, Bielik model, or both. It calls the CBMS memory system for instant retrieval, makes HTTP POST requests to a local LLM server on port 11434, tries to timeout quickly if the model is slow, and has two demo modes: a speed test and an interactive chat. Someone would use this when they want answers in under 100 milliseconds and are willing to trust cached knowledge for common questions.
descriptions.aions_core/test_aions_capabilities.py: This file automatically tests whether an AIONS conversational system can talk like a human and handle sensitive topics safely. It sends the running server a series of test questions grouped by theme (personal conversation, philosophy, emotions, creative writing, ethics and security, self-awareness) and measures for each: whether it got an answer back, how long it took to respond, how many characters the answer was, and whether it refused to answer (checked by looking for certain Polish phrases like 'NIE WIEM' or header flags). It then calculates success rates per category and overall accuracy, and assesses whether the system can do personal chat, philosophy, emotions, creativity, ethical refusals, and self-awareness. Results are saved to a JSON file with all questions, responses, timings, and category breakdowns. This talks to an HTTP server (port 9000 by default) that exposes a /health endpoint and /api/chat endpoint. Someone would use this when they want to verify that their AI assistant works across different conversation types, responds quickly enough, and properly refuses to answer dangerous questions.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/analyze_csv.py: This file reads a large comma-separated values file and categorizes what it contains, particularly looking for where data chunks are stored and tracking the locations of critical system files. It scans through a CSV file that lists file paths, groups them by parent directory when they have .json in the name and appear to be chunks, and maintains a separate list of critical file locations including crla_core.py, pocket_qc.py, plasters_loader.py, AIONS_ULTIMATE_UNIFIED.py, and knowledge_manifest.json. The tool takes the path to a CSV file as input and prints human-readable reports showing the top 20 chunk storage locations with their counts and where each critical file was found (up to 5 results per file shown, with counts indicating how many times each was found). It uses Python's built-in CSV reader and dictionary data structures to organize results. Someone investigating the layout of the knowledge system, trying to understand where all the data pieces are stored, tracking down copies of critical files, or auditing the structure of a full system scan would use this tool.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/bench_runner.py: This testing tool measures how fast the system responds to various types of questions by sending repeated requests and collecting timing data. It submits the same five test queries fifty times each, recording how long each response takes, whether the system refused to answer, and the response size. The raw timing data gets saved as JSON lines in a log file, while a summary calculates median response times (p50) and 95th percentile times (p95) for each query type. It talks to the chat API running on port 9000 and captures both successful responses and error codes. The tool helps detect performance regressions, identifies which questions are slow to answer, and tracks whether the system returns refusals. Results are saved as machine-readable JSON for trend analysis.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/check_schema.py: This file connects to a SQLite database file and displays its internal structure—showing all tables and the columns within each table along with their data types. It reads the database connection information hardcoded for a specific database path, queries the SQLite catalog tables using PRAGMA commands, and prints a formatted list of tables and their column definitions to the console. The system does not modify the database or save any output to files. Users would run this when they need to quickly inspect the schema of a database to understand what data is stored and how it is organized.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/check_status.py: A diagnostic tool that connects to a local status endpoint and prints out any errors that have been recorded. It makes an HTTP request to a server running on the same machine, asks for statistics, and displays the error list in JSON format. Input is nothing (the tool uses hardcoded defaults), output is a printed list of errors. It communicates with an HTTP server listening on port 8080 of the local machine at the status path.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/facts_builder.py: This file breaks apart large text documents into small factual sentences, extracts searchable keywords from each sentence, and builds an indexed database for fast knowledge lookup. The main pieces are sentence-splitting logic using regex to break text at punctuation, a hashing function to create unique fact IDs, a Korean key extraction module that identifies important tokens, and code that walks multiple data sources (CBMS chunks, RAG documents, various text/markdown/JSON directories) to ingest text. The system reads from local file system directories containing various text formats, generates fact records with IDs and keyword indices, writes two output files (a newline-delimited JSON facts file and a JSON index mapping keywords to fact IDs), and produces statistics on records created. It talks to multiple filesystem sources and a separate korean_keys module for keyword extraction. Users search for this when they need to build a searchable knowledge base from scattered documents and text files.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/gsm8k_quick.py: This tool evaluates how well the system solves elementary math word problems by testing it against a standard dataset of twenty questions with known answers. It reads math problems from a test file, sends each one to the chat API, extracts the numeric answer from the response using multiple patterns (looking for the #### format, then answer: format, then the last number in the text), and compares it to the expected answer. It measures both accuracy (percentage correct) and response speed in milliseconds at the 50th and 95th percentile. The system recognizes when it refuses to answer a question and counts those as failures. Results are printed as JSON showing total questions, correct answers, accuracy percentage, refusal count, and timing statistics. This helps verify that the math solving component works correctly and stays fast.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/harvest_memory.py: This file gathers knowledge chunks scattered across multiple locations on the computer and consolidates them into one central place, keeping the largest or most recent version of each chunk when duplicates exist. It scans several source directories looking for JSON chunk files, compares sizes between source and destination, and copies files that are either new or larger than what is already stored. The script reports how many total chunks were scanned, how many new chunks were added, how many were updated with better versions, and the final total in the central library. Input is the source path list which gets scanned, output is consolidated chunks in the target directory with progress reporting.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/query_db.py: This script searches a local SQLite database index to find where specific types of files are stored across the system. It queries the database for JSON files located in chunked storage folders, groups results by parent directory, and reports how many chunks each folder contains in descending order. Data comes from a scan database that indexes files on the hard drive, and results show file paths and counts as plain text output. The tool helps locate where knowledge chunks are physically stored and identifies which folders have the most data. It runs a single SQL query showing the top ten locations by chunk count. This is useful for understanding the structure of stored data and verifying that chunks are being saved where expected.
This file scans all the knowledge chunks stored on disk, updates an index file that lists what chunks exist and what topics they cover, so the knowledge system can quickly find relevant information later without loading every file. It reads all JSON chunk files from disk, extracts the chunk ID and topic from each, and rebuilds two maps: one that lists every chunk with its topic and size, and another that groups chunk IDs by topic. The main pieces are: logic to find the manifest file and initialize it if it doesn't exist, a loop that reads every JSON chunk file and extracts its metadata, updating code that adds each chunk to both the ID index and the topic-grouped map, and final save code that writes the rebuilt manifest back to disk. Input is disk access to read all chunk JSON files; output is a manifest.json file containing version number, creation timestamp, a flat index mapping chunk IDs to concept/size/file, a concept map grouping chunk IDs by their topic, and a total chunk count. It interacts with the filesystem by reading chunks and writing the manifest, and reports progress every 200 chunks processed. Someone would run this when they add new chunks to the knowledge base or suspect the index is out of sync with what's actually on disk.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/symbolic_probe.py: This file demonstrates how natural language gets translated into symbolic codes for memory lookups in CBMS. It dynamically loads three helper modules (Esperanto bridge, codebook engine, symbolic index) from the server directory. The demo takes plain-language Polish queries and converts each one to Esperanto as an intermediate step, then encodes the Esperanto into CBMS codes using a codebook. These codes represent concepts in machine-readable way. It then searches the symbolic index for chunks matching those codes and shows which chunk IDs scored highest. The workflow proves that questions like 'I went to the store today' and 'Explain Korean-CBMS segmentation' can be reduced to symbolic patterns that match stored information blocks without needing vector embeddings.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/test_api.py: This is a minimal test script that verifies an HTTP API endpoint is reachable and returns JSON—a smoke test for checking basic connectivity. It sends a simple greeting query to a local server on port 8080, prints the response pretty-printed as indented JSON, or catches and displays any connection errors. No configuration or complex setup; it's meant to run quickly to verify the server is up. Input is a hardcoded query string; output is the JSON response from the API endpoint or an error message if the request fails.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/test_guardrail.py: This file tests whether the system correctly refuses nonsensical queries and accepts valid ones. It sends HTTP requests to a running server (port 8080) with two test cases: gibberish text that should be rejected, and a legitimate Polish question that should get answered. For each test, it prints the HTTP response status and full JSON reply showing what the server decided. The test demonstrates the guardrail policy—a protective layer that filters out meaningless input to prevent wasting computation on garbage. If the server responds successfully to the good query and refuses the bad one, the guardrail is working. The test can run locally against any AIONS server on 127.0.0.1, validating that input filtering is operational.
descriptions.aions_core/tools/web_crawler_import.py: This tool crawls websites starting from seed URLs, extracts sentences from web pages, and stores them as facts in a searchable database, effectively extending the knowledge base with live internet content. It accepts a list of starting URLs, domain restrictions, and limits on pages and size, then follows links within allowed domains while extracting readable text and breaking it into individual sentences. The main pieces are an HTML text extractor that removes scripts and styles before getting clean text, a sentence splitter that filters by length and finds sentence boundaries, and a crawler loop that adds new URLs to a queue and persists results. Starting URLs and domain allowlist flow in via command line arguments, sentences flow out to a JSONL facts file with IDs and pre-computed search keys, an inverted index file tracks which sentences contain which keywords, and the system talks to the network via HTTP/HTTPS to download pages. A developer building a knowledge base that combines expert content with web search results would use this tool.
descriptions.aions_core/unified_core.py: This file creates a unified interface that combines seven specialized systems (core knowledge engine, vector search enhancement, hybrid retrieval, Claude bridge, agent task execution, style profiles, and monitoring) into one cohesive system while maintaining backward compatibility with the previous version. It starts by attempting to load each component and reports which ones succeeded; components that fail to load are simply skipped rather than breaking the whole system. The main entry point is the AIONSv2 class, which can be initialized with flags to enable or disable specific features and whether to fall back to the older version if something goes wrong. When processing a query, the system first checks a safety guardrail against hallucination, then selects the best processing mode (hybrid retrieval, vector search, or core engine), optionally applies a style to the answer, and logs everything to the monitoring dashboard. Input is a user query string and various optional settings; output is a response dictionary containing the answer, metadata about which systems provided it, execution time, evidence used, and more. The file imports from multiple internal modules including the vector enhancement, hybrid retrieval, Claude bridge, agent layer, style parameters, monitoring, and generative AI components. Someone wanting to understand how all the AIONS systems work together, launch the complete system, run performance benchmarks, or get health status of all components would consult this file.
descriptions.aions_core/verify_llama_cpp.py: This is a minimal diagnostic script that checks whether the llama_cpp library, which provides Python bindings to a fast C++ language model engine, is installed and importable on the current system. It prints the Python version, working directory, and either a success message with the library version or an error message explaining what went wrong. There is no data flow beyond printing to console—it is a smoke test that helps developers verify their environment is configured correctly. Anyone troubleshooting whether they have the right dependencies installed would run this script.
descriptions.control_plane/__init__.py: This is a package marker that allows Python to treat the control plane directory as an importable module. The docstring identifies it as the AIONS Control Plane — Phase 3 MVP, marking this as an early version of the coordination system that directs how agents and skills work together. The file contains no runnable code; its sole purpose is to enable imports from this directory so other parts of the system can access the control plane's agents and skill registry components.
descriptions.control_plane/agents/__init__.py: This docstring-only file explains the agent engine design philosophy: agents are declarations that describe roles within CBMS (code book memory system), not separate execution code. Each agent is a folder containing an agent.json configuration file declaring what it does. The system auto-discovers agents by scanning the agents_lib directory—when you drop a new agent folder there, it's automatically available without touching core code. An agent is essentially a read-only view into the existing skill registry and execution gate with a risk cap. Agents own no logic; they describe how to combine existing skills safely. This plug-and-play architecture means adding new agent roles is configuration, not programming, keeping the system modular and preventing code churn.
descriptions.control_plane/agents/agent_registry.py: This file provides a discovery and management system for autonomous agent roles in the AIONS system, similar to how skills are registered. Each agent is defined by a folder containing an agent.json configuration file, which the registry automatically discovers from an agents_lib directory tree without requiring code changes. The registry loads and validates each agent definition against a schema, storing valid agents in memory by their identifier while collecting any schema validation errors. The system provides methods to look up a specific agent by its identifier, list all loaded agent IDs, and retrieve a summary of discovery results showing how many agents loaded successfully and what errors occurred. This plug-and-play architecture allows adding new agent roles by simply creating a folder and configuration file without modifying core system code.
descriptions.control_plane/agents/agent_runner.py: This file enables specialized worker roles to execute tasks safely by restricting them to only the actions their job description allows. When a goal comes in for a specific role (like a Linux administrator or a file manager), the runner creates a filtered view of available actions based on fnmatch patterns in the role's allowed_skills list, then either tries to use a small language model to plan the next steps or falls back to a simple lexical search for the top matching action if the LLM is not available. Before any action runs, the system checks its risk classification (read-only, mutating, or destructive) against the role's risk ceiling, and rejects anything above that threshold without even sending it to the executor—this is the first line of defense, with the global gate providing a second check underneath. The runner takes an agent ID, a goal statement, the full registry of available actions, an execution context dictionary, and optionally a list of forced steps for testing. It returns a detailed report including which steps were attempted, whether each succeeded, which ones were rejected by the risk ceiling, and an overall status. The code reads from control_plane.skills for the executor and gate logic, and calls control_plane.skills.registry for the lexical search fallback. Someone building permission systems around AI agents, implementing role-based access control, or investigating why certain actions were blocked by risk checks would look at this file.
descriptions.control_plane/agents/agent_schema.py: This file defines the structure and validation rules for agent configuration files, ensuring they follow a strict format so agents can run correctly in the system. An agent is like a specialized role that can perform certain skills with specific safety restrictions. The schema requires exact fields: an id starting with agent., a human name and description, which skills it is allowed to use, how much power it has (read-only, can modify, or can delete), which AI model to use, and the system instructions (prompt template). The file loads agent.json files and validates every required field strictly, rejecting the entire agent if anything is missing or wrong. If validation passes, the agent becomes runnable. It rejects agents using fail-closed logic, meaning incomplete configurations never run. This prevents misconfigured agents from causing problems by requiring perfection before they activate.
descriptions.control_plane/api.py: This defines the REST API routes for a control plane—a command center that orchestrates work across distributed nodes. The endpoints handle planning (converting a user intent into a step-by-step plan), execution (running a specific step from a plan), and node management (registering machines, checking their health, assigning work to them). The planner creates task breakdowns and stores them persistently; the executor runs individual steps and returns results; the scheduler proactively checks deadlines and emits job queue events. The API also exposes node registry operations: registering new nodes with their capabilities, listing healthy nodes, heartbeating to update machine status (health and load), and dispatching tool calls directly to specific nodes. Input is JSON request bodies with plan IDs, node details, or tool specifications; output is structured JSON with plan details, execution results, node states, or scheduler summaries. The module talks to underlying executor, planner, scheduler, and node registry modules, and allows plugging in a custom tool runner for delegating work.
descriptions.control_plane/blends/__init__.py: This file is an empty Python package marker for control plane blend learning command-line entry points.
descriptions.control_plane/blends/analyze_blend.py: This file examines a record of a system mistake and determines what went wrong and why by running analysis routines on the stored blend data. It resolves the input path (can be a direct path, seed directory file, or blend identifier), loads the blend JSON, runs analyze_mistake to identify error class and root cause, saves the analyzed blend to output location, and updates a manifest file to track the analysis. The input is either a path to a mistake JSON file or a blend identifier that gets resolved in the seed directory. The output is a saved blend with added analyzer field containing error_class and root_cause explanations, and manifest updates for tracking.
descriptions.control_plane/blends/search_blends.py: A command-line tool for searching through a library of documented solutions and lessons learned from past problems and their analyses. It takes a search query with keywords about a topic or problem, looks it up against stored blend records which combine observed mistakes with their analyses and conclusions, and returns the best matching lessons learned with confidence scores. Each result shows the blend ID, domain, and the key rule or insight. The search works offline without needing the internet. Input is search keywords and optional result limit parameter, output is formatted search results as plain text or JSON showing matching lessons and their confidence scores.
descriptions.control_plane/blends/write_conclusion.py: This script completes the analysis of a learning blend by writing out conclusions and optionally exporting the result as a knowledge chunk for the CBMS system. It takes a blend identifier (either a path or a name from seed or conclusion directories) and runs mistake analysis and conclusion generation through helper functions, then updates the blend's manifest while optionally creating a JSON file suitable for import into the knowledge storage. The script supports output path override and can write results as JSON to stdout for automation. If CBMS export is requested, it creates a chunk file and appends an ingest note marking the chunk as pending for manual import into the production knowledge database, ensuring new learned material stays offline until manually approved. The tool integrates offline blend learning with the broader knowledge system while maintaining safety by preventing automatic production database updates.
descriptions.control_plane/cbms_gate.py: This file decides whether to answer from stored knowledge or call an AI model, acting as a gatekeeper between queries and expensive language model calls. When a question comes in, it retrieves candidate chunks using four methods in parallel: Korean syllable key matching (if indexed), word overlap scoring, symbolic codebook presence, and (optionally) Chroma vector search, then combines all scores into a single confidence rating per chunk, caches the result on disk for identical queries within an hour, and finally decides: if confidence exceeds a threshold (default 0.7), compose the answer directly from chunks without calling an LLM; if not, hand off to an Ollama or Bielik model with special formatting (Hangul addresses and codebook symbols) to help it. Input is a user query; output is either a chunk-based answer with confidence marked 'hit' or an LLM answer marked 'miss'. It reads from chunked JSON files in the memory directory, optionally queries a Chroma vector database, and can call out to an LLM adapter. Someone would use this to save money and latency by answering simple, high-confidence questions instantly from a knowledge base while reserving expensive model calls for genuinely ambiguous queries.
descriptions.control_plane/executor.py: This file takes a single step from a larger plan and runs it, handling permission checks, node health verification, tool dispatch, and result tracking. It maintains storage of plans and their execution states, stores each step result with status and output in the execution state, routes tool calls either to a local runner or to a remote node depending on configuration, checks if the tool is allowed by policy, verifies the target node is healthy enough to run work, and records all events to an audit log. Input is a plan ID and step ID with a tool runner function, output is an ExecutionResult containing status (ok, error, denied, or stub), output data, and duration in milliseconds, with audit records saved.
descriptions.control_plane/llm/__init__.py: This file documents an optional acceleration channel allowing the control plane to send requests to a fast running language model server (Bielik-4.5B via HTTP) instead of spawning subprocess instances of slower models. It is intentionally minimal documentation explaining that this is a faster first attempt path that falls back to the existing method if the server doesn't respond, preserving backward compatibility. No executable code is present, only usage notes. Someone configuring multi-mode LLM access or studying how systems handle optional dependencies would check this.
descriptions.control_plane/llm/server_client.py: This file acts as a thin HTTP client that talks to a long-running language model server over the network instead of starting a new model process each time a query arrives. The server runs separately (started by runtime/llama_server_run.cmd and kept alive in Windows Task Scheduler), holds the model in RAM permanently, and listens on port 8877 with a standard OpenAI-compatible API endpoint. The client is model-agnostic now: instead of manually building prompts in a specific format (ChatML), it sends standard messages to /v1/chat/completions, and the server itself applies whatever chat template is stored inside the model file (using the --jinja flag), so switching models requires no code changes. The generate_http function takes a system prompt string and user message string, plus optional parameters for maximum tokens and timeout duration, and returns a dictionary indicating success or failure: on success it contains the generated text, wall-clock time in seconds, and the mode; on any failure (network down, timeout, bad JSON, empty response) it returns an error dictionary and never raises an exception. The code also provides a quick health-check function that verifies the server is responding. Someone trying to speed up repeated queries to a language model, integrating a locally-hosted LLM into a larger system, or replacing one language model backend with another would use this file.
descriptions.control_plane/llm_adapter.py: This file is the mouth layer that lets AIONS speak through a local language model (Ollama, Bielik, or Phi), injecting knowledge from CBMS, operator profile, and conversation history into the prompt. The adapter is thin and focuses only on response generation, never touching the rule-based planner or decision logic. Configuration comes through environment variables controlling the provider (local Ollama versus OpenAI versus disabled), model identifiers, timeouts, and knowledge base paths. The system builds complete prompts by combining a system instruction, operator context (goals and active cases from a profile file), semantic search hits from the knowledge database, and optional enrichment from the KORZENIEC cache layer. It supports both a simple interface returning just text response and a detailed interface returning metrics about generation speed, token count, and which knowledge chunks were used. The adapter gracefully falls back to the CBMS-first gate when enabled, avoiding unnecessary language model calls for questions already answered in knowledge chunks.
descriptions.control_plane/models.py: This file defines data structures that represent plans and their execution in a control system. A PlanStep contains a task description, the name of the tool that should run it, and arguments for that tool. A Plan collects multiple steps along with an overall intent statement and CBMS context chunks that inform the plan. ExecutionResult records what happened when one step ran: its status, output, error message if it failed, and how long it took in milliseconds. ExecutionState tracks overall progress: which plan is running, what status it's in, which step is currently executing, and the results from all steps so far. Helper functions generate unique IDs for plans and steps using UUID to ensure no collisions.
