descriptions.control_plane/node_agent/agent.py: This file is a lightweight daemon running on Linux worker machines that registers with central control, sends regular health updates, and accepts remote commands to execute shell operations. It gathers host metrics from Linux system files (/proc/loadavg for CPU, /proc/meminfo for memory, statvfs for disk), builds an HTTP server listening for POST requests with commands, authenticates requests using a token header, executes commands with timeouts up to 60 seconds, and returns exit code plus stdout and stderr output. The agent reads configuration from a JSON file specifying node ID, core URL, token, bind address and port, logs all activity, and independently retries registration to core if connection fails while continuing to serve requests locally.
descriptions.control_plane/node_dispatch.py: This file determines whether a tool step should run locally in the current process or be sent to a remote machine for execution, and generates the appropriate response structure. It maintains a list of known local nodes and checks whether an incoming request targets one of them by checking node IDs or host addresses against a whitelist of localhost variants. For local nodes, it runs the tool immediately using a provided runner function and returns the result; for remote nodes, it returns a stub containing the target URL and message that remote execution isn't live yet. Requests flow in with a node ID and tool name, responses flow out as JSON with mode (local/remote), status, and either results or target URL. A developer building a distributed computing system or federating computation across machines would need this.
descriptions.control_plane/node_registry.py: This file maintains a list of available worker machines in the system, tracking what each one can do, whether it is healthy, how busy it is, and what permissions it has, so tasks can be routed to the best machine for each job. It keeps this registry in memory with optional saving to disk as JSON, loads the registry at startup from a saved file if it exists, and creates a default local development node if the registry is empty. The main pieces are: a NodeRecord dataclass holding one machine's ID, hostname, capabilities list, memory amount, available tools, health status, load percentage, and permissions; functions to register new machines or update existing ones; functions to list all nodes or find the best node for a specific task; and persistence code that reads from and writes to a JSON state file. Input is registration calls with machine details or heartbeat updates with current health and load; output is NodeRecord objects and query results showing which machines are available and healthy. It reads and writes to a JSON file in a configurable state directory, detects whether it is running on Windows or Linux to set default capabilities, and implements staleness checking so stale heartbeats can be ignored. Someone would use this as the component that decides which backend machine should handle a particular request.
descriptions.control_plane/operator/__init__.py: This file is a package initializer that re-exports a set of functions from a loop module, making them available as the main public interface for the operator control system. It exports observe (to read system state), diagnose (to detect problems), act (to fix issues), verify (to confirm the fix worked), learn (to record what happened), run_cycle (to execute one full loop), and main (to start continuous operation). Input is implicit in the loop module implementation; output is the re-exported functions. It talks only to the sibling loop module. Someone would import this when they want to set up an autonomous operator loop that continuously watches a system, detects what's wrong, tries to fix it, and learns from results.
descriptions.control_plane/operator/loop.py: This is the operator automation loop that runs continuously to detect and fix system problems. It follows a five-phase cycle: observe (collect system stats), diagnose (identify issues), act (take corrective steps), verify (confirm issues are resolved), and learn (save incident record). The observe phase gathers memory usage, disk usage, failed services, and error log counts using shell skills. Diagnose applies threshold rules—if disk is over 90%, if a service failed, if load average is too high, or if error counts spike. Act recommends fixes or takes automatic action like restarting a service with safeguards like restart cooldowns. Verify re-observes to check whether the fix worked. Learn saves incident records to JSON log, optionally adding LLM commentary in Polish when actions escalate to human review.
descriptions.control_plane/operator/mouth.py: This file adds human-readable commentary to system incidents after the operator has already decided what to do, using a language model to briefly explain what probably happened and suggest a next step. The operator loop makes all decisions deterministically (about whether to restart services, scale up resources, or escalate to a human), and this module's only job is to attach a short, 1-2 sentence explanation that helps a human operator understand the context. The code is designed to never raise exceptions—any failure (missing model, LLM timeout, subprocess error, bad response) simply returns None, and the operator loop continues unchanged whether the commentary is present or not. It first tries to use a always-running Phi-4-mini server on port 8877 (via server_client.py) to avoid the overhead of loading the model fresh for each incident, and if that server is down or too slow, it falls back to running the model via subprocess (llama-cli.exe). The comment_incident function takes a dictionary containing issues and actions already decided by the deterministic operator, extracts the most important parts into a brief description (up to 5 issues and 5 actions), and sends that to the LLM with a system prompt requesting a concise comment in the language of the incident report if possible, otherwise in English. It returns the comment string or None if anything failed. Someone implementing human-friendly incident reporting, adding LLM commentary to automated system operations, or coordinating between deterministic rules and optional AI explanations would find this file useful.
descriptions.control_plane/orchestrator_loop.py: This file implements the core AIONS loop: understand the user's intent, retrieve relevant facts from the knowledge base, compose an answer using only what was retrieved, and optionally store the exchange in memory for learning. It chains together several subsystems—the LLM-based mouth for parsing intent, the CBMS gate for retrieval, and optional Chroma vector database for memory storage. The main flow receives a natural language query, extracts the user's intent (language, whether they want to be remembered), retrieves matching knowledge with confidence scores, decides whether the retrieval was successful, and speaks a response grounded only in what was found. User queries flow in via command line or the `run_local` function, JSON results flow out to a file containing understanding, facts, spoken answer, and performance metrics, and the system coordinates with mouth.py, cbms_gate.py, and an optional server.store memory helper. Someone building a retrieval-augmented generation system or studying how to keep language models honest would study this.
descriptions.control_plane/planner.py: This file takes a user's stated intent and decides which system should handle it, then creates a step-by-step plan with specific actions to accomplish the goal. The main pieces are an intent validation function, regex pattern matching to classify the intent type (health check, search, memory recall, or knowledge lookup), a step creation process that builds specific actions with parameters, and node selection logic that picks which compute resource should run the plan. The system accepts an intent string and optional node ID, attempts to retrieve knowledge context from the CBMS memory system if available, creates a plan with unique IDs and timestamps, and returns a structured plan object with steps and metadata. It talks to the CBMS memory system for context retrieval and a node registry for resource selection. Users search for this when building a reasoning system that needs to decompose high-level goals into executable steps.
descriptions.control_plane/policy.py: This file defines which tools an operator is permitted to call and which commands are forbidden, acting as a simple allow-list and block-list system. The allowed_tools frozen set lists exactly seven tools that may be called: system_health, cbms_search, memory_recall, fast_search, aions_plan, aions_execute_step, and aions_execution_status; any other tool name is automatically blocked. The check_intent function screens user statements for dangerous patterns like 'rm -rf /', 'format c:', or 'delete all' and rejects any intent containing those substrings. Both functions return a tuple of (boolean, string) indicating whether the action is allowed and a reason message. There is no persistent state, network calls, or file I/O—this is purely an in-memory gate that can be checked before any action executes. Someone implementing a permission system for constrained execution, building policy controls for autonomous operations, or maintaining a list of blocked operations would consult this file.
descriptions.control_plane/scheduler.py: This file builds a queue of scheduled work by reading an operator's profile and pulling out deadlines with due dates, active cases, and daily recurring tasks like morning briefings. It loads an operator profile JSON that contains lists of deadlines and active cases with due dates, collects all items falling within a lookahead window (default 14 days), creates ScheduledJob objects for each deadline and case reminder, marks urgent items due within 3 days separately, and emits events to an audit log. Input is the operator profile JSON located at a known path, output is a SchedulerSummary with job queue, deadline list, and events, used to surface what needs attention to the operator.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/__init__.py: This is a package marker file that declares the skills module as part of the AIONS Skill Engine. It contains only a single docstring describing the module's purpose for unified object and skill management. The file serves to make Python treat the directory as an importable package with no additional runtime initialization needed.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/context.py: This file builds an execution context (a small whitelist of safe helper functions) that individual skills can call when they run, without skills needing to directly manipulate global state or the operating system. The context includes a file finder (using the Windows Everything search tool if available), a note saver (appends JSON records timestamped), app launcher and closer (using Windows subprocess with detached windows), and get/set state functions for global variables. Input is optional extra functions passed in as a dict; output is a context dict with all helper functions plus an empty 'bag' for skills to store temporary data. This depends on Windows Everything.exe being installed, writes notes to a state directory, and manages a simple key-value store. Someone would use this when building a skills framework where you want each skill to have only the powers it actually needs, with a central audit trail of what it did, rather than giving every skill full system access.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/executor.py: This file runs skills—reusable action bundles—one at a time or in chains, with each step's output available to later steps, and it blocks skills from running if certain system conditions are currently true. It resolves references like '$bag.key' in input values so output from one skill can feed into another, checks whether the skill's state conditions (avoid_when) prevent running, sends the skill through a security gate, times the execution, catches errors, and records everything in an audit log. The main components are the reference resolver, the state condition checker, the security gate integration, and the step recorder. Skill IDs and input dictionaries flow in, and JSON results containing status, runtime, and either output or error messages flow out, while the system talks to gate.py for security decisions and world_state.py for environment conditions. A developer building a task automation system with safety constraints would use this.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/forge.py: This file manages the full lifecycle of skill blocks—accepting requests for new capabilities, verifying that newly-built code is safe and functional, and promoting it into the live library. The main pieces are request management (writing pending requests to disk), promotion logic that validates skill JSON schema and executes the Python code to verify it works, sandbox verification for Linux-based skills using a remote VM, and safe file movement between directories (pending, built, done, failed). The system reads skill request JSON files and handler.py files from built directories, validates them through schema checking and code compilation, optionally tests them in a Linux sandbox environment, then either promotes them to the live skills_lib or moves them to failed. It also includes gap detection logic that examines whether existing skills already cover a stated intent. The file talks to the file system, a schema validation module, a Python compiler, and optionally a Linux VM sandbox verifier. Users look here when building a system that needs to safely add new capabilities without trusting unverified code.
This file implements the verification pipeline for Linux-targeted skills before they can be deployed to production nodes. When a new skill candidate is proposed through the forge system (identified with a linux.* prefix), the system runs four sequential checks: validation that the skill.json configuration file matches the required schema and declares a risk level, compilation of the Python handler using py_compile to catch syntax errors, sandbox execution where low-risk skills are run live against a test virtual machine via SSH while higher-risk skills only receive a dry-run echo command, and logging of the complete verification result to both the remote machine and a local record file. If any check fails, subsequent checks are skipped to fail fast. The entire verification report, including which checks passed and why any failed, is returned to the caller and stored in the forge verification log for audit purposes.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/gate.py: This file is a security checkpoint that decides whether to allow a skill to run based on its declared risk level and whether it has pre-approval. It classifies skill risk into three levels (read-only is always allowed, mutate is logged, destructive requires a non-expired approval entry), then checks whether the skill is approved if needed, and finally appends a JSON record to a per-node, per-day audit log with the decision, timestamp, skill ID, and a truncated copy of inputs (to keep logs from bloating). Input is skill metadata (including risk level and ID), the inputs being passed in, and the node name (which computer is running this); output is an allow/deny decision and audit metadata. It reads an approvals.json file to check current permissions and writes append-only JSONL audit files. Someone would use this to enforce that high-impact operations (like deleting files or modifying configs) can't run without manual sign-off, while keeping read operations fast and allowing mutating operations with just logging.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/goal_planner.py: This file is the decision-making core where a small local language model (Phi-4-mini) selects and chains skills from a catalog to accomplish goals, operating entirely within constrained choice from a provided list with no hallucination of undefined skills. The planner implements multiple layers of caching before calling the expensive language model: first checking for exact-match recipes from previously learned solutions, second searching the CBMS knowledge database for similar goals with cached solution steps, third doing semantic recipe matching for paraphrased intents, and only if all caches miss does it query the language model. Each step has hard validation ensuring selected skills exist in the registry and input parameters match the skill schema, filtering out hallucinated placeholder values like "<host_name>" or empty strings. The goal execution function runs the planned skill chain through a risk gate, then if successful and learning is enabled, saves the goal-and-steps as a recipe for future reuse. All decisions about cache hits, LLM calls, and why chains succeeded or failed are logged and returned to the caller.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/mcp_bridge.py: This file exposes the skill engine to MCP tools by wrapping skill execution, search, and planning functions. It re-discovers the skill registry on every call so newly added skill files are picked up automatically without restarts, making the system truly plug-and-play. The main functions list all available skills with descriptions, search skills by keyword, run individual skills with inputs, execute multi-step recipes, and list saved recipes. Skill IDs and input dictionaries flow in, skill metadata and execution results flow out as JSON, and the system talks to the skill registry, executor, planner, and recipes module. Someone exposing a skill system to MCP clients or studying hot-reload patterns would examine this.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/papiery.py: This file manages personal administrative items as JSON blocks stored directly on disk with no external database, following the same philosophy as CBMS where everything is a self-contained file. Each item (paper/task) is created with a title, optional deadline, notes, priority level (high/normal/low), and tags, and receives a generated identifier based on the title and creation timestamp. The system provides methods to list all open items sorted by deadline and priority, find items due within a specified number of days, search items by text in title or notes, and mark items as done with a completion timestamp. Stored items live in a directory on the user's E: drive and can be searched with command-line tools, backed up with file operations, and integrated into workflows as plain JSON.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/planner.py: This file decides how to execute a task by checking if there is a cached recipe for that kind of task, and if not, gathering available skills that can help solve it and filtering out any that cannot run right now. It is very short and delegates the hard work to recipe lookup and world state checking. The main pieces are: a call to find a matching recipe based on the task intent, a search through available skills if no recipe exists, per-skill checking of whether world conditions block that skill from running, and return of either a recipe to replay or a list of candidate skills for a stronger model to compose into a plan. Input is a registry of available skills and an intent string describing what the user wants; output is a JSON structure containing either a recipe ID and steps, or a list of candidate skills with information about which ones are currently blocked by world state. It calls recipe lookup and world state matching functions, and is designed to be called by a planner orchestrator that has access to the skill registry and current environment state. Someone would think of this as the part that finds the right tools or cached procedures for a job.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/recipes.py: This file stores learned success recipes for recurring problems as verified skill chains plus context about why they worked and the world state when they succeeded. A recipe is saved only after successful execution passes verification, capturing the goal, ordered steps, and reasoning snapshot. The system bridges recipes with the CBMS knowledge database by semantically indexing each new recipe in a Chroma session so that paraphrased goals (different words, same meaning) can match cached solutions without waking the language model, with a measured threshold of 0.70 confidence to avoid false matches. The core storage is a single JSON file tracked in git, with recipe lookup by an identifier derived from the goal text and reuse counting for statistics. Storing into Chroma fails gracefully without breaking the local JSON persistence.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/registry.py: This file automatically discovers and manages a library of runnable skills (plugins) by scanning a folder for skill.json manifest files, loading them into memory, and supporting fast search. Each skill is a folder with skill.json (describing what it does, what inputs it takes, what risk it has) and optionally handler.py (the Python code that runs it). When searching for a skill by keyword, it uses a lightweight stemmer that removes common English plurals and Polish grammatical endings, then normalizes Polish diacritics, so that a query for 'services' matches a tag 'service' and 'usługi' (Polish) matches 'usługa'. Input is a search query and optional type filter; output is a ranked list of matching skill IDs with scores. It reads JSON files from disk and dynamically imports Python handler modules. Someone would use this when they want to build a plugin system where non-programmers can drop a folder into a library directory and have it automatically be found and callable, without needing to edit core code.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/schema.py: A data definition file that describes what an AIONS object looks like and what fields are required for different types of things the system can do. It defines a single unified model (AObject) that represents any skill, recipe, workflow, knowledge item, or decision rule with fields for identification, type, description, requirements, handlers that execute them, and risk level. It validates that each object has the right fields for its type—for example, executable skills need a handler function, and recipes need steps. Input is a path to a JSON file or structured data to load, output is an AObject instance or a list of validation errors. The file is purely structural; it defines the schema and provides functions for loading and validating objects.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/semantic_search.py: This file enables finding the right action or skill by meaning, not just by matching words, by blending semantic similarity from vector embeddings with traditional keyword matching in a calibrated way. The module went through four iterations (v2 through v4) tuning weights and selecting embedders using a test set of 131 queries (48 original, plus 92 expanded with multilingual Polish cases, plus 39 new English cases), split once-and-frozen into tune and held-out evaluation halves. Each version improved on specific weaknesses: v2 fixed false positives by rejecting semantic-only candidates below a higher threshold; v3 tested a multilingual embedder but failed its accuracy gate (61.5% top-1 vs 64% bar); v4 achieved 87.5% on the held-out set by adding English descriptions and utterances to the indexed content while keeping the default embedder. The public semantic_skill_search function takes a query string and returns a list matching SkillRegistry.search's format, blending lexical token overlap (scored by term count, normalized to a saturation point) with semantic cosine similarity (0 to 1) using tuned weights, with separate acceptance thresholds for candidates found by both methods versus semantic-only candidates. Input data comes from the SkillRegistry (list of available skills with tags and descriptions) and the Chroma vector database (indexed documents with embeddings). Every Chroma call is wrapped in try/except, so if the database is down, the function silently degrades to pure keyword search. Someone building a skill finder that understands natural language paraphrases, tuning retrieval for multilingual queries, or investigating why a specific query matched or missed an expected skill would look at this file.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/stats.py: This file tracks how well automated skills or tasks perform over time by recording success rates, execution speed, and calculated confidence scores. Each skill gets performance statistics stored in JSON, with counts of successful and failed attempts, average execution time in milliseconds, a calculated success rate percentage, and a blended confidence score that weighs reliability against speed. The confidence calculation prioritizes reliability by default but can be adjusted to prefer speed instead via a preference parameter. Data is stored persistently in a JSON file under the runtime directory, loaded on demand and saved after each recorded execution. It talks to Python's pathlib and json modules to manage file storage. Someone would ask about this when they need to pick between multiple ways to solve a problem and want to choose the fastest reliable one, or when tracking whether automated systems are working well.
descriptions.control_plane/skills/world_state.py: This file maintains a live JSON snapshot of the current state of the system—which applications are open, whether the user is logged in, which services are running, etc. The main pieces are load and save functions that read/write the state from disk, a get/set interface for reading and updating individual state variables, a matches function that evaluates conditional expressions, and a default state template with keys for browser, moodle login, notepad, git, docker, WSL, internet, and VPN status. The system reads and writes a single JSON file in the runtime directory, supports string equality and inequality operators in condition checking, and treats certain values as falsy (unknown, closed, logged_out, etc.). It talks to the file system for state persistence and the skill execution system which reads this state to avoid repeating actions. Users search for this when they need a simple shared record of what's currently happening in the system so different components don't duplicate work.
This is a wrapper script that launches an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for VS Code—a bridge allowing Claude to read and interact with code files through standard input/output protocol. The script fixes a directory issue where VS Code doesn't properly change working directories on Windows, ensuring the server runs from the correct path so it can find its modules. It imports the actual MCP server implementation and starts it in stdio transport mode, which means all communication happens through piped streams rather than network sockets. No configuration needed beyond ensuring the hardcoded path points to the right directory.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/__init_: This file is the main entry point that launches an MCP server with configurable transport (HTTP or stdio). It loads configuration from environment variables for logging level and port, then starts the server using either HTTP streaming mode on a configurable port or standard input/output mode depending on the transport_type parameter passed at startup.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/__main_: An entry point that starts an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server allowing remote clients to connect and use AIONS as a code analysis tool. It checks that the Python environment is inside a virtual environment to prevent accidental system-wide installation, handles Windows-specific fixes for standard input and output, and launches the server in one of three network modes: direct pipe communication for local use, HTTP for optional remote LAN access, or special event-stream protocol. The server accepts environment variables to configure networking options and security settings. Input is command-line arguments and environment variables, output is a running MCP server accepting JSON-RPC protocol requests. It coordinates with the actual server implementation and handles cross-platform network setup.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/desktop: This file provides remote control capabilities for a Windows computer through multiple functions: taking screenshots, clicking the mouse, typing text, pressing keyboard keys, launching applications, scrolling, focusing windows, running shell commands, and reading/writing the clipboard. All operations run on a dedicated single worker thread to avoid blocking the MCP async event loop. The main pieces are lazy dependency checking for required libraries (mss, pyautogui, win32 modules), window enumeration functions that list visible windows with titles and process names, target resolution logic that converts app names to executable paths, and individual implementation functions for each operation type that handle parameter conversion and error handling. The system accepts parameters for screen position, key combinations, text content, window titles, and shell commands; performs the requested operation; and returns status and result information. It talks to the Windows API through pywin32 modules, uses pyautogui for mouse and keyboard control, mss for screenshots, and win32clipboard for clipboard access. Users search for this when building systems that need to automate Windows desktop interactions like clicking UI elements, opening applications, or capturing screen content.

This file provides a unified interface for controlling a desktop across Windows and Linux platforms, letting higher-level code take screenshots, click, type, scroll, and manipulate windows without worrying about the underlying OS. It defines a base class with abstract methods, then provides concrete implementations—WindowsDesktopProvider that wraps a native desktop_control module, and LinuxDesktopProvider that combines wmctrl for windows, xdotool for input, and mss for screenshots. The main pieces include capability reporting (which features are available), timeout wrapping for safety, error handling that raises DesktopProviderError, and method implementations for each action. Commands like 'click at X,Y' or 'type this text' flow in, responses with status and coordinates or output flow out, and the system talks to platform-specific tools and libraries. An automation engineer or bot builder targeting multiple operating systems would use this.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/filesys: This file creates and maintains an index of all files and directories in specified folders, allowing very fast file searches without scanning disk every time. It builds a JSON index file containing every file and folder path found, with metadata like size and modification time, then answers search queries by looking in the index instead of walking the directory tree. The main pieces are: configuration for which root directories to index and which folders to skip (like .git and node_modules), index generation code that walks the file tree and creates entry dictionaries for each file and folder, search functions that match query text against stored paths and rank them by how well they match, and staleness checking so the index is refreshed automatically if it gets too old. Input is a search query string or file extension filter and a max results limit; output is a list of matching file paths ranked by score. It reads the filesystem to build the index, stores the index as a JSON file with customizable location and refresh interval, and compares queries against file names, paths, and relative paths with different scoring for exact match, prefix, substring, or path match. Someone would use this to search for files by name or pattern much faster than the operating system file search.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/llm_mou: This file is a thin speech adapter for AIONS that translates between user language and the system's internal decisions, using a Qwen language model as the voice but never inventing facts. It has two main functions: 'understand' which parses user text into structured intent (language detected, whether AIONS should search memory or codebook or web, whether to remember this question), and 'speak' which rephrases AIONS-provided facts into a short, natural reply in the user's language, strictly using only the facts given and preserving special tokens (like addresses and symbol codes). It can run on either Ollama (a separate service on port 11434) or in-process llama.cpp (GGUF model), with automatic fallback to the other if one is down. Input is text for understand or facts for speak; output is JSON with intent details or a natural language reply. It depends on Ollama or GGUF infrastructure and talks to the aions_gguf_runner experiment module for in-process operation. Someone would use this when they want an AI system that talks to users but is guaranteed not to hallucinate facts, because it's only allowed to rephrase verified knowledge.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/patched: This file fixes a Windows buffering bug in MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that causes multiple JSON-RPC messages to get batched together when they should arrive separately. The server creates an async transport layer over standard input and output that reads incoming messages line-by-line and writes outgoing messages with explicit flush and small delays to prevent bundling. Two background tasks run continuously: one reads messages from stdin and converts them to MCP session messages, the other takes session messages from a write queue and sends them to stdout with a deliberate small pause between messages. It uses anyio for async I/O and the mcp library for message parsing and serialization. Someone would need this when running an MCP server on Windows and finding that Claude receives multiple tool responses as a single batch instead of individually.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/provide: This module selects and configures platform-specific backends for filesystem search and desktop automation—like choosing between different engines for finding files or controlling the screen. It decides whether to use Everything (Windows fast search), AIONS Linux indexing, or no search if neither is available; it also creates platform-appropriate desktop automation providers (Windows via UIAutomation, Linux native). Functions like resolve_search_provider_name choose the best available search backend based on what's installed, while get_desktop_provider returns a platform-specific desktop controller. Additional utility functions like search_provider_status and desktop_provider_capabilities expose the current configuration and capabilities for health checks and documentation. Input includes platform name strings and feature flags; output is provider instances and capability dictionaries.
This is a comprehensive MCP server that provides Claude with access to the host computer's tools and data. It integrates file searching through Windows Everything or Linux indexing, Docker and container management, WSL Linux distribution control, Git version control commands, network diagnostics like ping, a file scanner that analyzes project structure and dependencies, conversation logging with automatic batching to ChromaDB and JSON logs, memory storage and retrieval through vector search or Korean-key matching, CBMS knowledge base chunk retrieval, Google Calendar event reading, and system health monitoring. Each tool call gets automatically logged to a buffer that dumps when full, creating an immutable record of what Claude tried to do. The server discovers tools like Docker and Git from the system PATH or common installation locations, uses configuration from environment variables for features like HTTP vs embedded vector database backends and search paths, and provides context guards that compress large responses into references to save Claude's token budget. It talks to dozens of external systems including the local filesystem via Everything.exe or Linux indices, Docker daemon, Git repositories, WSL distributions, the operating system for shell commands, ChromaDB for vector storage, CBMS for semantic chunk retrieval, Google Calendar API for events, and the mcp library for protocol handling. Someone would ask about this when they need Claude to interact with their computer's files, run commands in containers, check Git history, search the disk quickly, or store and recall important context across sessions.
descriptions.mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/test_se: This file is the simplest possible test version of an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, used to verify that the protocol works at all and the basic infrastructure is in place. It creates a FastMCP server instance, registers three trivial tools (ping returns pong, echo bounces back the message, and health returns server status), and runs via standard input/output transport. The main purpose is smoke-testing: confirming that the FastMCP library imported correctly, that tool registration works, and that the server can start and process basic requests. It prints debug messages to standard error at each step to help diagnose where something fails if it doesn't work. There is no persistent state, no database calls, and no external dependencies beyond the MCP server library. Someone new to the MCP server system, debugging why the integration isn't working, or setting up a minimal example to build from would start with this test server.
descriptions.scripts/aions_healthcheck.sh: This script is a diagnostic tool that checks whether all parts of an AIONS installation are working correctly, intended to run regularly (e.g., from cron or a scheduler). It verifies that the repository is accessible, systemd user services are running, Python environment setup is valid, the Chroma vector database library is installed with its version, and (on Linux) the search indexer and optional API server are responding. It also outputs system information like repository path and Python version. Input is environment variables (CHROMA_PATH, PYTHONPATH); output is a log of check results written to a file. It calls sub-scripts (aions_python.sh, verify_python_env.py, aions_indexer.py) and optionally makes HTTP requests to an API endpoint if AIONS_API_BASE_URL is set. Someone would use this when they need to know at a glance whether an AIONS system is healthy or degraded, what services are up, and what's broken, so they can quickly spot and fix problems.
descriptions.scripts/aions_indexer.py: This file builds or refreshes a searchable index of the entire Linux filesystem by scanning specified directory roots and cataloging what files exist where. It accepts a command (refresh to rebuild, status to show info, or ensure to only refresh if stale), takes root directories to scan and an index file path, and uses a filesystem provider that auto-refreshes when the index gets older than a threshold (default 15 minutes). The index gets saved to a JSON file and includes information about which files are where for fast searching later. Input is command line arguments specifying roots and output path, output is the generated index JSON and status information printed to standard output.
descriptions.scripts/aions_node_heartbeat.py: A monitoring agent that periodically sends health-check signals to a central coordinator service so it knows this machine is still running and working properly. It sends POST requests to a core API every 60 seconds by default, reports the node's health status and current CPU load percentage, and logs any network failures to standard error. It can read the node ID from configuration files or environment variables, allowing it to identify itself to the coordinator. Input is configuration such as node name, API address, and check interval, output is log messages and periodic network requests to the core API. It communicates with the AIONS core API over HTTP using JSON-formatted POST requests.
descriptions.scripts/aions_python.sh: This file is a bash launcher that finds and uses the correct Python virtual environment from configuration, so all AIONS scripts use exactly the same Python version and installed packages regardless of where they are called from. It reads configuration from a file that specifies which Python version and which venv directory to use, verifies that the venv exists and has the right Python version, creates the venv if needed, and then either shows the path to Python or executes a command with that Python. The main pieces are: config file reading that parses key-value pairs and extracts the Python version and venv path, version verification that actually runs Python to check it matches expectations, venv setup code that creates a fresh venv and installs dependencies from a requirements file, and mode handling to support resolve-only, ensure-venv-only, or run-command modes. Input is command-line arguments like --resolve to print the path, --ensure-venv to set up if needed, or Python arguments to execute; output is either the Python executable path printed to stdout or execution of a Python command with that interpreter. It reads the python.env configuration file from the .aions directory, checks Linux and Windows paths depending on platform, and looks for a fallback config if the main one is not found. Someone would use this as a safe wrapper ensuring that when they run AIONS Python scripts in any shell context, they always get the environment they expect.
descriptions.scripts/aions_tray.py: This file creates a small icon in the Windows system tray (the notification area in the bottom-right corner) that shows whether Claude Desktop is running and offers quick-access menu options to restart it, kill it, start it, open log files, or open the configuration file. The tray icon is green if Claude is running and red if it is not, with an 'A' for AIONS displayed inside. A background thread refreshes the icon status every 5 seconds so it always stays current. The right-click context menu provides six actions: Restart Claude Desktop, Stop Claude Desktop, Start Claude Desktop, Open Logs, Open Config, and Exit Tray Manager. The code finds Claude.exe in the standard Windows location (LocalAppData\Programs\Claude), checks running processes using psutil to detect whether Claude is already running or not, and launches or kills it using subprocess calls. The log file path is read from environment variables (Claude's logs folder), and the configuration file is looked for in the AppData\Claude directory. Someone needing quick controls to restart Claude without using the command line, monitoring whether Claude is still running, or accessing Claude's logs and configuration without hunting for folders would use this script.
descriptions.scripts/calendar_e2e_smoke.py: This file tests whether the Google Calendar connection is working correctly by fetching today's and tomorrow's events, listing the next 10 upcoming events, verifying date range queries work, and checking that the OAuth token can refresh successfully. It verifies that OAuth credentials and token files exist in expected locations, imports Google libraries, makes actual API calls to retrieve events, formats output to show what was found, and tests the token refresh mechanism with force refresh. All tokens and credentials are kept private and never printed. Input is the existing OAuth configuration and saved token file, output is formatted event listings and status messages confirming the calendar is accessible and token refresh is working.
descriptions.scripts/catalog_e_treasures.py: This script creates a machine-readable inventory of all the knowledge data and backup copies stored across different hard drives and folders in the system. It scans thirteen different treasure locations, measuring how many files are in each, total size in gigabytes, and how many data packs they contain. It also reads the main knowledge manifest to report how many knowledge chunks are in the active system. The script generates a JSON catalog file with metadata about each treasure location including whether it is currently connected and being used, and notes about its purpose. It outputs the timestamp when the catalog was generated, the generator script name, and summary statistics. This helps understand what data exists where, whether it is archived or active, and how much storage space each collection uses.
descriptions.scripts/chatgpt_extractor.py: This script reads the ChatGPT Desktop application cache to extract conversation history, custom GPT configurations, and user information. It parses binary LevelDB database files from two cache locations, converts the binary data to readable text, and uses pattern matching to find conversation IDs, titles, timestamps, and message content fragments. It saves results as JSON summary files, plain text chunks, and a markdown report showing all recovered conversations. The script also performs deep extraction by dumping raw cache contents to separate text files to capture any readable strings missed by pattern matching. Data comes from the encrypted ChatGPT cache in Windows AppData, and output goes to a folder with multiple report formats. The tool helps recover conversation history when ChatGPT data needs to be archived or analyzed outside the official application.
descriptions.scripts/chatgpt_parser_v2.py: This file extracts structured data from a large raw text export of ChatGPT data by finding patterns that match conversation titles, user information, and message content using regular expressions. It searches for patterns like conversation IDs paired with titles in JSON format, looks for items in arrays, searches through conversation history blocks, and extracts readable titles near UUIDs. It also pulls out user display names, user IDs, email addresses, and organization identifiers from the raw text, finds all things that look like conversation titles using multiple regex patterns, and attempts to extract message fragments from content fields. Output is a JSON file with structured conversations, all found titles, user information, and message fragments, plus a markdown report summarizing the extraction.
descriptions.scripts/chatgpt_ultimate.py: This script extracts everything stored in ChatGPT Desktop's local cache files and produces a clean inventory. It reads raw LevelDB text dumps and parses them with regex patterns to find user emails, display names, user IDs, message counts, conversation titles, custom GPTs the user created, draft messages, and model access information like GPT-5 availability. Some data is stored as spaced-out text (each letter separated by spaces), so the script reconstructs normal words. It generates two output files: a JSON file with all extracted data organized by category, and a markdown report showing conversation history, model access levels, and custom GPT list. The script handles encoding issues and malformed data gracefully, keeping everything readable.
descriptions.scripts/demo_papiery.py: This demo script shows how to use CBMS blocks to manage personal tasks and reminders like a digital secretary. It loads the skill registry which discovers all available CBMS blocks, then adds sample papers (tasks) with titles, deadlines, and priority levels. The secretary then lists all stored papers, finds papers due soon (within 7 days), and sends a system notification reminding the user of urgent items. The script also searches for papers matching a keyword. Finally, it demonstrates how the skill registry's search function picks the right CBMS block for a question by returning the best match. All task data lives in local JSON files within your CBMS directory, not in a remote database. The demo proves CBMS blocks can replace apps for task management.
descriptions.scripts/demo_secretary.py: This script shows the skill engine in action by running a practical workflow: a morning status briefing, a system notification popup, learning a new multi-step recipe by example, opening Gmail in the browser, testing skill retrieval on real queries, and showing a summary of performance. The workflow demonstrates building a context object (workspace for state), discovering available skills from the library, executing individual skills in sequence (get current time, system info, open windows, recent files, RAM usage, send notification), running a multi-step chain to create a note with the current timestamp and count its words, saving that chain as a reusable recipe if it succeeded, and searching for skills by intent (e.g., 'co mam otwarte' for 'what do I have open'). It reads from a skills library, builds an execution context, runs skills through an executor with verification steps, stores successful sequences as recipes, and prints statistics about how many skills succeeded and how many recipes are available. Someone learning how to use the skills engine, testing whether skills work end-to-end, or understanding what multi-step workflows look like would read this script.
descriptions.scripts/demo_skill_live.py: This demonstration shows how the system learns to combine multiple small actions into reusable recipes and then uses those recipes again instead of planning from scratch. It opens applications, checks if they are already open to avoid repeating actions, runs a multi-step task like finding a file and saving a note about it, verifies the result, and stores that sequence as a reusable recipe. The script loads available skills from a registry, executes them with planning and learning logic, and tracks success statistics. On the second attempt with the same intent, it retrieves the saved recipe instead of replanning. It demonstrates that the system improves with repeated tasks and learns state awareness (knowing when applications are already open). The output shows which skills loaded, execution times, verification results, and whether the system passed by correctly learning and reusing the recipe.
descriptions.scripts/demo_train.py: This file demonstrates the complete skill learning workflow: teaching the system how to perform tasks by composing steps, verifying the composed steps work correctly, saving successful sequences as reusable recipes, and tracking performance metrics. The main pieces include skill registry discovery that loads available capabilities, step composition that chains multiple skills together, execution and verification of step sequences, recipe saving that remembers successful patterns, and statistics monitoring that shows which skills work reliably and which are used most. The system exercises three learning scenarios: writing log files with timestamps, creating folders and zip archives, and creating desktop shortcuts. For each scenario it runs the steps, verifies success by checking disk state, saves the successful sequence as a recipe if verified, then shows how planning changes before and after learning. The system reads from local directories to access skills, writes output files to the workspace, and tracks success/failure statistics in memory. Users look for this when understanding how skills can be combined and learned from successful execution patterns.
descriptions.scripts/demo_windows_batch2.py: This script runs a hands-on demo of the skills engine on Windows by executing a chain of tasks in sequence (create a folder, write a file into it, list the folder contents, test clipboard operations, fetch system IP and network status, take a screenshot, open a web browser) and showing the result after each step. It uses the skill registry to discover available tasks, builds an execution context with helper functions, and runs a verification callback (checking whether files actually got created) to confirm the system learned a new recipe. It then shows a monitoring summary of how many times each skill succeeded or failed. Input is paths and text to write; output is console messages and potentially new recipe definitions saved to disk. It imports from control_plane and depends on the skills_lib folder containing skill.json manifests. Someone would run this to test that the skills framework is working end-to-end on their Windows machine, that files can be created, web pages opened, and system info retrieved, and that the learning system can save recipes.
descriptions.scripts/demo_windows_final.py: This file demonstrates the complete skill execution system working end-to-end by creating multi-step workflows, executing them, and learning new recipes from successful runs. It discovers all available skills in a registry, uses a planner to create step sequences from natural language intent, runs the steps using an executor that handles file operations and system commands, verifies success by checking if expected outputs were created, and if successful, saves the workflow as a reusable recipe. The demo creates test folders, writes files, zips directories, opens folders in explorer, searches the web, checks system resources and disk space, adjusts volume, types text into notepad automatically, and monitors success rates and performance across all executed skills.
descriptions.scripts/demo_windows_session.py: This file demonstrates a complete monitored session where the system orchestrates real Windows desktop tasks: opening Notepad, writing and displaying poetry, closing the application, and gathering system information, while continuously tracking what it learns. The main pieces are skill registry loading that discovers available capabilities, search and selection logic to pick the right skill for each task, step composition for multi-step workflows, recipe learning that saves successful task sequences, and performance monitoring that shows skill success rates and confidence levels before and after execution. The system loads a poem from disk, performs four tasks (open editor, write and display poetry, close editor, show system info), learns a new recipe for the write-and-display workflow, verifies it works by checking disk state, and shows before/after statistics on skill performance. It reads poems and system state from disk, displays results on screen through application automation, saves recipes and statistics to the runtime state, and launches applications through the desktop control system. Users look for this when learning how automated systems can accomplish real tasks on a computer while building and reusing knowledge.
descriptions.scripts/full_system_scan.py: An orchestrator that inventories all files across all hard drives, analyzes code dependencies and project structure, and generates a master report showing which projects exist on the system. It runs in three phases: first it gets a complete file list per drive using the Everything search tool, then it runs detailed code analysis per drive to find dependencies and duplicates, and finally it detects project roots by looking for markers like .git or package.json files. Input is optional drive letters to scan in order (defaults to all except special backing volumes), output is CSV inventories, detailed scan reports, and a master map JSON file with all discovered projects and their locations. It uses the Everything desktop search tool to enumerate files and runs subprocess commands for the turbo scanner analysis.
descriptions.scripts/hello_world.py: This file is a simple test script that prints 'Hello World' to the console and exits with a success code, designed to verify that the test framework and Python environment are set up correctly. The main pieces are a hello_world function that handles the print operation with error handling, and a main entry point that catches exceptions and exits with the appropriate status code. The system takes no input beyond command-line invocation, prints a fixed message to standard output, and exits with code 0 on success or 1 on failure. It talks only to the console and Python's sys module for exit codes. Users run this when testing whether a new Python environment or test harness is working before attempting more complex operations.
descriptions.scripts/ingest_tier1_chroma.py: This script loads high-priority knowledge from the CBMS chunk store and operator profile into a Chroma vector database for semantic search—turning raw chunks into queryable embeddings. It verifies the chromadb version matches (0.5.x), loads the operator profile and chunk manifest, filters out plaster chunks (special utility chunks), and selects a curated tier-1 sample including priority chunks like bootstrapping and CBMS access rules. The script formats operator data as readable text and creates index summaries, then either runs in dry-run mode (showing what would be ingested) or actually adds items to named Chroma sessions. Input is JSON files containing the manifest and operator profile; output is a vector store with operator metadata, CBMS index samples, and concept chunks indexed by embedding space. The script enforces that only the production chromadb version 0.5.3 can write to the database, preventing compatibility issues with newer versions that use incompatible binary formats.
descriptions.scripts/ingest_treasures_tier2.py: This file reads a catalog of important files and folders stored elsewhere on disk, converts that catalog into searchable summaries, and stores those summaries in a vector database so the system can later find relevant treasure data by searching for keywords. It does not copy the actual files—just their metadata, paths, types, and descriptions. The main pieces are: a catalog loader that reads from a catalog JSON file, formatting code that turns each catalog entry into a readable summary with path, type, status, and file counts, metadata builders that attach proper tags and timestamps, and vector store code that saves the summaries to Chroma database collections. Input is a JSON catalog file containing treasure entries with paths, types, file counts, and status; output is the summaries stored in two Chroma collections: one for system operators and one for the user's knowledge base. It checks the Chroma version to ensure it is the 0.5.x format compatible with the production database, reads and parses the catalog JSON, interacts with the VectorStore class to perform the actual storage, and can run in dry-run mode to show what would be stored. Someone would run this after updating a catalog to make that metadata searchable in the knowledge system.
descriptions.scripts/operator_daily_brief.py: This script generates a morning briefing for a system operator that reads their profile and outputs a personalized summary of active cases, upcoming deadlines, goals, and recent decisions, optionally including a system health check and scheduled task status. It loads an operator profile from a JSON file (containing identity, active cases with status, deadline list with due dates, goals with priorities, and historical decisions), formats it as readable Polish text with status and priority labels, calculates how many days until each deadline, and appends optional health checks and scheduler output. Input is command-line flags (--health, --horizon, --emit-scheduler, --json) and an operator profile JSON file; output is formatted text or JSON depending on the flag. It imports from a scheduler module that manages tasks and deadlines, and can optionally run the scheduler to emit task events. Someone would use this when they want an operator to get a one-page morning update automatically showing what they need to focus on that day, what's overdue, and whether the system is healthy.
descriptions.scripts/operator_profile_load.py: This script reads the operator profile file that stores information about who is using the system, loading it from the canonical knowledge storage location. It first tries to find the knowledge directory using an environment variable, then checks standard locations on different drives. If the profile exists, it reads the JSON file and returns the profile data; otherwise, it reports an error. The profile can include information like the operator name, preferences, roles, and other identity information. This helps the system know who it is talking to and can be used to personalize responses or apply user-specific access controls. The script resolves paths across both Windows and Linux-style mount points to work in different environments.
descriptions.scripts/project_scanner.py: This is a comprehensive file analyzer that scans source code repositories, extracts dependencies between files, detects duplicates and broken links, and generates reports—like a code archaeologist mapping relationships between parts. It walks directory trees, reads each code file, extracts imports and references using language-specific parsers (Python AST, JavaScript regex, JSON/YAML), computes MD5 and SHA256 hashes to find duplicates, and builds forward and reverse dependency graphs. The scanner detects orphaned files (nothing imports them), hub files (imported by many others), broken imports that can't be resolved, and circular dependencies. Output includes JSON files with all scan data, a dependency graph, a list of orphans and hubs, and a human-readable markdown report summarizing findings. Input is one or more file paths to scan; the system ignores standard directories like node_modules and git folders. The tool produces time-stamped result directories with comprehensive analysis useful for understanding architecture complexity.
descriptions.scripts/proof_provenance.py: This script acts as a smoke test to verify that every piece of information stored in memory carries audit metadata (where it came from, who stored it, which machine, which session, when). It connects to the MCP server via HTTP, calls the memory_store tool with a test message, then queries the ChromaDB database directly to retrieve the metadata for that stored record and checks that all six required fields are present: agent (which system wrote it), host (which computer), surface (which interface), run_id (which execution), os (operating system), and era (timestamp). It exits with code 0 only if all required fields are found, making it suitable for use in automated deployment pipelines. The test writes through the live HTTP endpoint but reads directly from ChromaDB by importing the chromadb library, so it verifies the full path from API to storage layer. Someone implementing a compliance or audit system, verifying that metadata capture is working, or testing memory storage before deployment would run this script.
descriptions.scripts/register_treasure_chunk.py: This file registers a catalog of data storage locations into the knowledge system so the AI can find important datasets when searching for information. The main pieces are catalog loading from a JSON file containing treasure metadata (location, type, status, size), content generation that formats the catalog into a readable text description, chunk creation with metadata (ID, concept tag, size, timestamps, references), and manifest updating that indexes the new chunk for retrieval. The system reads a treasure catalog JSON file and creates a knowledge chunk file, or updates it if already registered, then updates a manifest index file that tracks all chunks. It saves files to the memory chunks directory using safe atomic writes with UTF-8 encoding. It talks to the file system for reading catalog data and writing chunk and manifest files. Users search for this when they need to register important datasets or resource catalogs into the knowledge system so searches can find them.
descriptions.scripts/run_mcp_server.sh: This shell script sets up the environment and launches the AI Model Context Protocol server in either stdio or http transport mode. It establishes Python environment variables for UTF-8 encoding, disables telemetry, sets paths to Chroma vector database and AIONS workspace directories, resolves the correct Python executable using the aions_python helper script, changes to the server directory, and executes Python with the server module. Input is an optional transport mode parameter (stdio or http, defaults to stdio), output is a running server process that communicates over the specified transport channel.
descriptions.scripts/set_aions_cache_env.sh: A configuration script that sets up directory locations for temporary files and downloaded packages, redirecting them from system defaults to a specific development folder on the D drive to keep the system drive clean. It configures environment variables for pip package cache, Python temporary files, Hugging Face machine learning model downloads, PyTorch library cache, Docker configuration, and other development tool caches, all pointing to centralized paths under a single AIONS cache root. This approach organizes all development caches in one place and prevents clutter on the system drive. Input is nothing or the AIONS_CACHE_ROOT environment variable override, output is set environment variables and created directories ready for use by development tools.
descriptions.scripts/smoke_http_mcp.py: A quick test that verifies an AIONS MCP server is running and responding correctly over HTTP protocol. It sends a standard initialization handshake to the server asking it to identify itself and list available tools, reads the response, and checks if both the handshake and tool listing succeeded. It demonstrates that the server is alive and the network protocol works properly. Input is optional URL parameter defaulting to local port 8787, output is printed status messages showing server name and tool count plus exit code 0 for success or 1 for failure. It communicates with an HTTP endpoint using JSON-RPC protocol with server-sent events, making raw HTTP requests.
descriptions.scripts/sync_dev_mirror.sh: This script is a one-way file synchronizer that mirrors the live knowledge server from Windows drive E: to a development mirror on a WSL (Linux subsystem) drive D:, using rsync to copy only changes and optionally delete extra files in the destination. It excludes certain large or generated folders (Python virtual environments, vector database cache, scan results, compiled Python) to keep the mirror small and fast, and can optionally include or exclude the .git folder. Input is environment variables (AIONS_SYNC_SOURCE, AIONS_SYNC_DEST) or command-line flags (--dry-run to preview changes without copying, --mirror to delete files that don't exist in source, --include-git to copy version history); output is rsync statistics showing how many files changed and transfer progress. It depends on rsync being installed and both source and destination being accessible. Someone would use this when they need to keep a development copy in sync with a live server without manually copying files, so they can test changes locally before updating production.
descriptions.scripts/test_control_plane.py: This script performs a smoke test of the control plane locally and optionally checks a remote API health endpoint via an SSH tunnel to a guest machine. It creates a test plan for 'check health', stores it, executes one step using a mock runner, verifies the execution completed, then attempts to reach a remote control plane API if a URL is provided. The main flow builds the test data locally, runs through the execution pipeline, then probes the remote endpoint with a timeout. Test parameters and optional remote URL flow in via command line arguments, success or failure status flows out to the console, and the system talks to the control plane's plan and execution modules. A developer verifying that the control plane works end-to-end or testing multi-host setups would run this.
descriptions.scripts/test_forge.py: This script tests the entire workflow for requesting, building, integrating, and using a new skill: it requests a skill called 'demo.hello', writes a fake built skill to disk with handler code, promotes it to the registry, runs it, checks for gaps in the registry, then cleans up the test artifacts. The main steps simulate what would happen if a language model built a skill in response to 'say hello', and the script verifies each stage works. Skill definitions flow out to JSON files and Python modules on disk, the registry discovers and executes the skill, and results flow to console output. A developer testing the skill forge pipeline or understanding how skills move from request to active use would run this.
descriptions.scripts/test_google_integration.py: This smoke test verifies that Google Cloud integrations for Gmail and Calendar are properly wired up without actually using credentials—checking that modules import, libraries are installed, and configuration functions work. It confirms scopes are read-write (not read-only), checks that configuration paths resolve within the secrets directory, and verifies that absence of credentials raises NotConfiguredError rather than crashing or silently failing. It also confirms that placeholder providers like Outlook are correctly rejected. The test doesn't need actual Google OAuth tokens or Gmail access; it just validates the integration skeleton is correct. Output is pass/fail with a message explaining any issues found, useful for CI/CD verification that integrations are properly set up.
descriptions.scripts/test_llm_adapter.py: This test verifies that the Polish language model (Bielik via Ollama) answers correctly and uses injected context. It defines test questions with expected keywords that prove context was used: 'Who am I?' should mention the operator's name from operator_profile.json, and 'What is CBMS?' should reference the chunked memory system with words like 'chunks' or 'memory'. The test runs each question, checks if the response contains Polish language indicators (Polish characters and common words), then checks if expected context keywords appear. If the model responds in Polish AND uses provided context, the test passes. The script handles Ollama server availability gracefully, reporting whether the model endpoint is reachable and which models are loaded.
descriptions.scripts/test_node_registry.py: This smoke test validates the Faza 6 node registry system both as an in-process library and through an optional HTTP API. The in-process test registers nodes with capabilities and tools, verifies that nodes can be retrieved and listed, triggers a plan creation and execution to confirm the registry assigns appropriate machines to tasks, and checks that heartbeat updates work. The HTTP smoke test attempts to register a node via REST API and list all registered nodes, skipping gracefully if the API is unavailable. The test expects at least one local node to exist by default and validates the full lifecycle of node registration, discovery, plan creation, and execution.
descriptions.scripts/test_skill_engine_foundation.py: This end-to-end test demonstrates the skill engine discovering reusable task blocks, chaining two of them together (find a file, then save a note about it), verifying results before learning, and replaying saved recipes—showing how tasks can be automated and reused. The test registers skills, searches for file operations, plans a multi-step task, executes it with input chaining (output from first skill feeds into second), checks verification criteria, saves a recipe if verification passes, then replays the recipe to confirm it hits the cache on the second planning attempt. Statistics tracking records success counts for each skill, and world state captures persistent changes. This demonstrates plug-and-play extensibility: new skills need no core changes, type-agnostic retrieval finds them, and recipes provide learning.
descriptions.scripts/test_skill_open_apps.py: This live demonstration launches real applications (Notepad and Calculator) through the skill engine while tracking whether they're open using world state—showing how skills can control the desktop without repeating work. It sets initial world state to closed, calls open_notepad, verifies it opened and updated world state, attempts to open it again and confirms the system skipped the redundant action, then opens Calculator as a different skill. The test proves that skills are aware of side effects and can be chained intelligently to avoid unnecessary operations. Expected output is that first app launch succeeds, second attempt on same app is skipped, and third call to different app succeeds.
descriptions.scripts/turbo_scanner.py: This file is a fast project file scanner that leverages the Windows Everything CLI search tool to instantly locate files instead of slow directory traversal. It scans code, configuration, and documentation files across specified folders or the entire indexed system, computing metadata for each file including MD5 hash, line count, and parsed imports (Python and JavaScript). The system detects duplicate files by comparing hash values, builds a dependency graph by resolving import statements to actual files, identifies hub files that many others depend on, and marks orphan files with no incoming references. Results are saved as JSON files containing summary statistics, detailed file information, duplicate groups, dependency graphs, and a markdown report with tables and analysis. The tool runs file processing in parallel threads for speed and generates output suitable for codebase auditing and optimization.
descriptions.scripts/validate_aions_tools.py: This script quickly validates that MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool functions work after code changes. It imports tool implementations from the server module and runs quick tests: search for Python files, search in specific folders, check system health, search the code book memory, retrieve facts from long-term memory, check git status, list WSL distributions, list Docker containers, check project scan status, check conversation status, list MCP servers, and check thinking process status. Each tool should return a response with status='ok' or status='completed'. The script counts how many tests passed and reports totals. This is a smoke test confirming the server can execute its tools—useful after changes to ensure nothing broke.
descriptions.scripts/vault/_core.py: This file implements AIONS local secrets storage using Windows DPAPI (Data Protection API) encryption for the current user account, with no external key management or cloud services. Encrypted blobs live in the runtime/secrets/vault directory (excluded from git), while the scripts that manage them are tracked. The system creates an operator marker on first use—a DPAPI-protected proof that a particular Windows user owns this vault—which is verified before any decryption to ensure the vault is only opened by the authorized user. Each secret is sealed by encrypting its content with DPAPI and an entropy value, then wrapping the ciphertext in a JSON envelope with metadata about the original filename, timestamp, and a unique vault identifier. The system maintains an index file listing all sealed secrets without exposing their plaintext. Sealing uses ctypes-based DPAPI calls with PowerShell fallback if ctypes fails, and all operations are offline with automatic file permissions set to owner-only.
descriptions.scripts/vault/open_secret.py: This command-line tool decrypts and retrieves secrets from the AIONS DPAPI vault for the currently logged-in Windows user. It can decrypt a specific vault entry by identifier and write plaintext to a file with locked-down permissions (mode 0600), or list all vault metadata (identifiers, labels, sealed timestamps) without exposing any secrets. The script is meant to be run locally by automation or the operator; agents and integrations should read the resulting plaintext files rather than trying to echo secret content to chat. Decryption fails if the operator marker is missing or invalid, preventing access from other Windows users.
descriptions.scripts/vault/seal_secret.py: This script encrypts plaintext secret files (like API keys or OAuth credentials) into a secure vault using Windows encryption so only the logged-in operator can read them. It takes a path to a plaintext secret file and a vault identifier, encrypts the file contents using the current Windows user's security key, stores the encrypted blob in the vault directory, and records metadata in an index file. After sealing, the plaintext file should be deleted to prevent accidental exposure. The script warns users never to commit plaintext secrets to git, and instructs agents never to echo file contents. It outputs the vault location, blob filename, and instructions for opening the secret again through a companion script. This protects sensitive credentials like Google OAuth client secrets from being leaked if source code is accidentally shared.
descriptions.scripts/verify_python_env.py: This script checks that the Python interpreter running it matches the version specified in AIONS project configuration—a guard rail ensuring reproducible behavior across different machines. It reads .aions/python.env, extracts the expected version, compares against the running interpreter, and reports platform, executable path, venv status, and Chroma database location. If versions don't match, it exits with an error. This prevents accidentally running AIONS with incompatible Python versions that might have breaking changes or missing dependencies.
descriptions.scripts/verify_tier1_chroma.py: This file runs tests to check that the vector database was set up correctly and contains expected data, doing a few searches to verify that the right information can be found. It does not modify anything, just reports on the state of the database. The main pieces are: code that initializes a connection to the Chroma database, functions that perform test searches on stored data like looking for operator profiles or CBMS keywords, code that retrieves statistics about how many documents are in each collection, and verification logic that checks whether the minimum expected numbers are met. Input is environment variables for the Chroma path if set, otherwise defaults to a standard location; output is a JSON report showing the Chroma path, list of available sessions/collections, sample search results from operator and main knowledge bases, statistics on document counts per collection, and a pass/fail result code. It calls VectorStore to connect to the database, performs actual search queries to verify data was ingested, checks that at least 2 documents are in the operator collection and 10 in the main collection and that searches return at least one result each, and reports all findings as JSON. Someone would run this after ingesting data to confirm that everything was stored correctly and can be retrieved.
descriptions.server/__init__.py: This is a Python package marker file indicating that the server directory is a Python package and can be imported.
descriptions.server/app.py: This is the main REST API server that manages a knowledge base with sessions, search, and document storage. Built with FastAPI, it listens for HTTP requests to add documents to a session, search for relevant documents, and manage sessions. Sessions are like workspaces—each one has its own collection of documents. The API provides endpoints to add context batches (text plus metadata), search using a query with optional filters, list all sessions with statistics, get details about one session, dump all documents from a session, prune expired documents, and view a dashboard summary. The server connects to a vector store (ChromaDB) that actually holds the data. CORS is enabled so clients from any origin can connect. Optional control plane routes can be added if available.
